units.title: Meaning, reference, and what speakers do with words

lessons.title: Sense and reference: Frege's puzzle, and why meaning is not just naming
lessons.explanation: This level turns from the evaluation of arguments to the materials arguments are made of: words, what they stand for, and what speakers do with them. The founding distinction is Frege's, stated in 'Über Sinn und Bedeutung' (1892), usually translated as 'On Sense and Reference'. Frege begins from a puzzle about identity. If 'a = b' is true, then a and b are the same object, so the statement says of an object that it is itself, which appears to be as trivial as 'a = a'. Yet many true identity statements are informative: they record discoveries, correct mistakes, and can be known by one person and not another. Frege's solution distinguishes two things a singular term contributes. Its reference (Bedeutung) is the object it stands for. Its sense (Sinn) is the mode in which that object is presented, the cognitive route by which a competent speaker latches onto it. 'Hesperus' and 'Phosphorus' refer to the same planet, so 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' is a statement of identity, but the two names present the planet differently, one as the evening star and one as the morning star, so the sentence joins two distinct senses and can be informative. Sense determines reference, not the reverse: a mode of presentation picks out an object, while an object can be presented in indefinitely many ways. Two consequences shape the rest of the level. First, there are no senses without a mind that grasps them, but a sense is not a private mental image: Frege insists that senses are objective and shareable, since communication would be impossible if each speaker's words carried a private picture. Second, sense is compositional: the sense of a sentence is the thought it expresses, built from the senses of its parts, and its reference is a truth value, so a sentence with a sense but a non-referring part may express a thought while failing to be true or false. This is a substantial theory with costs, and the costs are where the live disputes are.
lessons.example: Consider three sentences. (1) Hesperus is Hesperus. (2) Hesperus is Phosphorus. (3) The ancients believed that Hesperus was Phosphorus. Sentence (1) is a priori, uninformative, and knowable to anyone who knows the name. Sentence (2) was an empirical discovery, and a competent speaker could have understood both names and still denied it. If meaning were nothing but reference, (1) and (2) would say exactly the same thing, so the difference in cognitive value has to be located somewhere else, which is what sense supplies. Now the substitution test, which is the operational core of the distinction. From 'Lois believes Superman can fly' and 'Superman is Clark Kent' we may not infer 'Lois believes Clark Kent can fly'. The inference fails although the premises are true. Frege's explanation is that inside the scope of 'believes', the names do not stand for their ordinary references; they stand for their customary senses, so substituting a co-referential name substitutes a different sense and changes the thought attributed to Lois. Outside such contexts substitution is unrestricted: 'Superman is Clark Kent and Superman can fly, therefore Clark Kent can fly' is impeccable. The point is not that identity is unreliable but that semantic value is context-sensitive: a term can contribute its reference in extensional contexts and its sense in intensional ones. That is a strong claim, and it earns its keep by explaining a pattern of inference that otherwise looks arbitrary.
lessons.question: Lois believes Superman can fly, and Superman is Clark Kent, yet 'Lois believes Clark Kent can fly' may be false. What does Frege's account say the names contribute inside the belief report, and why does that block the inference?
lessons.answer: Inside the report the names contribute their customary senses rather than the man, so substituting a co-referential name substitutes a different mode of presentation and attributes a different thought to Lois
lessons.distractor: The names always contribute their reference, so the inference is valid and the second sentence is simply a false description of Lois's belief
lessons.correction: The distractor keeps a single semantic value for names in all contexts, which is the position Frege's distinction was introduced to reject, and then rescues the data by declaring a true premise false. The error is characteristic: rather than distinguishing two kinds of contribution, it denies the phenomenon. A learner who takes this route will also be unable to explain why the report sounds informative in the first place.

depth.definitions: A singular term is an expression whose job is to pick out an object: a proper name, a definite description, a demonstrative, an indexical. The reference (Bedeutung) of a singular term is the object it stands for; the reference of a sentence is, for Frege, a truth value. The sense (Sinn) is the mode of presentation of the reference, the content a competent speaker grasps when understanding the term. A thought (Gedanke) is the sense of a declarative sentence, the proposition it expresses. An extensional context is one in which co-referential terms are intersubstitutable without change of truth value; an intensional context, such as a belief report or a modal sentence, is one in which substitution can fail. Two further terms matter for what follows: psychologism is the thesis that logical and semantic facts reduce to facts about mental states, and Platonism about sense is the thesis that senses exist independently of any particular mind. Frege holds the second and rejects the first, and the combination is the source of much of the difficulty.
depth.mechanism: The argument has the form of an inference to the best explanation. Premise: some true identity statements are informative and some substitutions of co-referential terms change truth value. If semantic value were reference alone, neither fact could obtain, because identity of reference would guarantee sameness of content. Therefore semantic value must include something finer-grained than reference. Senses are posited as that finer-grained element, and they are individuated by cognitive significance: two expressions have the same sense only if a competent speaker who grasps both can recognise that they present the same thing without empirical investigation. Three structural features follow. Sense determines reference, so grasping a sense is sufficient for latching onto an object, which is why understanding a name requires more than knowing it names something. Senses compose, so the sense of a sentence is a function of the senses of its parts, which explains why speakers can understand novel sentences. And sense is objective, so two speakers can grasp the same sense, which is what makes disagreement possible rather than merely divergent association. Each feature is doing explanatory work, and each can be challenged separately, which is why the theory is best assessed as a package rather than as a single definition.
depth.secondExample: Frege's own case in 'Der Gedanke' (1918, 'The Thought') is a cleaner test than the astronomical one because it removes the astronomy. Two men, Herbert Garner and Leo Peter, both use the name 'Dr Gustav Lauben'. Garner knows Lauben as the man born on 13 September 1875 in a particular place, having been told this by Lauben's mother; Peter knows him as the doctor who lives in a particular house and attends him. Both names refer to the same man, so any sentence formed with the name and a predicate has the same reference whichever man utters it. Yet Garner and Peter do not know that they are speaking about the same person, and each would learn something from the other's information. Frege's diagnosis: the two names express different senses, so the thoughts they express differ even though the reference is shared. The case does more work than Hesperus and Phosphorus because nothing turns on a mistaken astronomical theory; the difference in sense arises from the ordinary social division of information. It also exposes a cost. If sense is what a speaker grasps, and Garner's grasp is exhausted by a birth record while Peter's is exhausted by an address, then the sense of a name varies from speaker to speaker, and it becomes unclear whether there is one shared sense at all. Frege's objectivity thesis is a commitment to there being a correct sense, not a derivation of it, and later theorists who treat senses as speaker-relative are making a different bargain.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first identifies sense with a mental image or a private association, which makes communication inexplicable and turns Frege into a psychologistic thinker he spent his career opposing. The second identifies Frege's sense with a definite description, so that 'Aristotle' means something like 'the teacher of Alexander', and then concludes that Kripke's modal argument refutes Frege. That is a misattribution: the descriptive theory of names is developed by Russell and by Searle, and Frege's sense is a mode of presentation whose relation to description is left open. A learner who merges the two will think lesson 104 has already disposed of Frege, when it has disposed of a different and more specific thesis. The third error is to treat the objectivity of sense as an embarrassment to be explained away, when it is a deliberate commitment: Frege needs shareable content to make logic normative for more than one thinker. Diagnostics: when a claim about Frege sounds like a claim about images or about disguised descriptions, check which of the three theses is actually being defended.
depth.application: Non-blocking task on paper. Choose three pairs of co-referential expressions, one pair of proper names, one pair consisting of a name and a description, and one pair of indexicals used on different occasions. For each pair, write four lines: the identity statement joining them; a belief report containing the first expression; the same report with the second expression substituted; and a verdict on whether the substitution preserves truth. Then, for each failure, state which sense difference explains it, using the test of cognitive significance: would a competent speaker who grasps both expressions need investigation to know they present the same thing? Model response for the name and description pair: the identity is true, the report 'she believes Cicero wrote the speech' may be true while 'she believes Tully wrote the speech' is false when she does not know the two names name one man, and the sense difference is that one name is associated with the orator's public career and the other with a family connection. Self-review rubric, four points: (1) each substitution is actually attempted rather than described; (2) the cognitive-significance test is applied to both expressions, not only the unfamiliar one; (3) failures are attributed to sense, not to the subject's ignorance alone, since ignorance is the datum the theory must explain; (4) at least one case is recorded where substitution succeeds, because a theory that predicted universal failure would be refuted by ordinary extensional reasoning.
depth.summary: Frege's distinction answers a narrow question, why some identities inform, and in answering it supplies a general picture in which meaning has two layers: an object stood for and a way of standing for it. The transferable move is to ask, whenever two expressions seem interchangeable, whether they present the same thing in the same way, and to expect substitution to fail wherever a sentence reports what someone thinks, believes, or might have done. The distinction also sets the agenda for the rest of this level, because the next three lessons press on each of its parts: Russell replaces the mode of presentation with a quantificational analysis of descriptions, Kripke denies that the sense of a name is descriptive, and Putnam locates part of meaning outside the speaker's head altogether.

lessons.title: Definite descriptions and logical form: Russell's analysis and the objections that survive it
lessons.explanation: Lesson 101 treated a singular term as having a sense that presents an object. Russell argued in 'On Denoting' (Mind, 1905) that this picture fails for a large class of terms and that the failure is instructive. A definite description is a phrase of the form 'the so-and-so'. On the face of it such a phrase is a singular term that stands for an object. Russell's proposal is that its grammatical form is misleading: 'the F is G' is not a subject-predicate sentence but a quantified one, analysable as: there is at least one F, there is at most one F, and whatever is F is G. In symbols, exists x (F x and for all y, if F y then y = x, and G x). Three consequences follow. Existence and uniqueness are asserted rather than presupposed, so a sentence whose description is empty is false rather than meaningless. Negation becomes ambiguous between the reading in which the existence claim is inside the scope of the negation and the reading in which it is outside, which is why 'the King of France is not bald' can be heard as either true or false depending on emphasis. And identity statements involving descriptions become analysable without positing senses: 'Scott is the author of Waverley' claims that exactly one person wrote Waverley and that Scott is that person. Russell's gain is that descriptions no longer require a special kind of entity to stand for them, which lets him deny Meinong's subsistent golden mountains without conceding that talk of them is meaningless.
lessons.example: Take 'the present King of France is bald'. Russell's analysis gives: there is exactly one present King of France, and he is bald. Since there is no such king, the existential conjunct is false, so the whole sentence is false. Its negation, read with the existence claim inside the scope of 'not', says that it is not the case that there is exactly one present King of France who is bald, which is true. Read with the negation inside, 'the present King of France is not bald' says that there is exactly one present King of France and he is not bald, which is false. The sentence is therefore not ambiguous in isolation but ambiguous in its possible readings, and the ambiguity is a scope distinction rather than a semantic gap. Compare Strawson's objection in 'On Referring' (1950). Strawson holds that 'the F' does not assert existence but presupposes it, and that presupposition belongs to the use of a sentence on an occasion rather than to the sentence itself. On that view, an utterance of the sentence when no king exists is neither true nor false, because the question of truth does not arise. The disagreement is not merely technical. Russell wants a determinate verdict so that the law of excluded middle holds and so that the falsehood can be asserted and denied in argument; Strawson wants to capture the intuition that a person who says it has not said something false but has misfired. Russell's reply, in 'Mr Strawson on Referring' (1957), is that ordinary usage is not the arbiter of logical form, and that the feeling of presupposition is a fact about the pragmatics of assertion, not about truth conditions.
lessons.question: A minute records that 'the chair of the safety committee approved the override', but the committee had been dissolved and had no chair. A member says the sentence is neither true nor false, so no finding can be recorded. Under Russell's analysis, what follows, and what does the difference from Strawson's view consist in?
lessons.answer: Under Russell's analysis the sentence is false, because it asserts that exactly one chair exists, and its wide-scope negation is true, so there is no truth-value gap to block a finding
lessons.distractor: Under Russell's analysis the sentence is neither true nor false, since a description that fails to denote cannot contribute an object and the whole sentence therefore lacks a truth value
lessons.correction: That is Strawson's conclusion, not Russell's, and attributing it to Russell inverts the theory's purpose. Russell introduced the analysis precisely to avoid both truth-value gaps and Meinongian objects, by converting the apparent subject term into a quantified condition. The learner's error is to treat the intuitive verdict about presupposition as common ground between the two theories, when it is the point at issue.

depth.definitions: A definite description is a noun phrase of the form 'the F', where F is a predicate. An indefinite description is 'an F'. Russell's theory of descriptions is the thesis that a sentence containing a definite description is true only if the description is uniquely satisfied, and that the sentence's truth conditions are given by an existential quantifier plus a uniqueness clause plus the predication. Grammatical form is the surface structure of a sentence; logical form is the structure that determines its entailments, and Russell holds that the two can diverge. A presupposition is a condition that must hold for an utterance to be assessable at all, as opposed to an assertion, which is a condition on the utterance's truth. A referential use of a description, in Donnellan's sense, is one in which the speaker uses the phrase to pick out a particular object and expects the audience to identify it; an attributive use is one in which the speaker asserts something of whoever uniquely fits the description. Scope is the range within which a quantifier or operator applies, and the ambiguity of negation in Russell's analysis is a scope ambiguity.
depth.mechanism: The analysis works by relocating existence from the subject position into the predicate. If 'the F' were a genuine singular term, the sentence would have a subject whose existence is a precondition of the sentence having a truth value, which is Strawson's picture and Meinong's temptation. Russell instead treats the phrase as a quantificational condition, so the sentence can be evaluated as false when the condition fails, without any commitment to a non-existent object. Uniqueness does the work that definite articles appear to do: 'the' signals that at most one thing satisfies the predicate, which is why a sentence with two satisfiers is false rather than merely uninformative about which one is meant. This yields a general test. Whenever a description appears in a sentence, ask which quantifier scopes over which operator, because the entailments change. The analysis also delivers a criterion of eliminability: any sentence containing a description can be paraphrased without it, which is what makes the theory a programme of analysis rather than a dictionary of meanings. The costs appear at the boundaries: descriptions in intensional contexts, descriptions used to refer to something that does not fit them, and plural or mass descriptions, all of which Russell's apparatus handles awkwardly.
depth.secondExample: Consider a construction contract stating that 'the surveyor appointed under clause 4 shall certify completion before payment falls due', and suppose no surveyor was ever appointed. Under Russell's analysis, the clause asserts that exactly one surveyor was appointed and that he certified, so the assertion is false; the consequence is that the condition for payment is not satisfied and the payment obligation does not arise. Under Strawson's account, the clause presupposes an appointment, so the question of compliance does not arise at all, and the parties are left with an incomplete agreement rather than a false certification. Legal practice often looks Strawsonian, because drafters insert severability and condition-precedent language precisely to specify what happens when a presupposition fails, which shows that the difference between asserting and presupposing has practical consequences for how documents are read. The case also exposes the limit of the analysis: the interesting question is not whether the clause is false but which obligations survive, and that question is settled by doctrine about conditions, not by the semantics of 'the'. The semantic analysis tells you where the truth value goes; it does not tell you what to do.
depth.mistake: The first error is to conclude that Russell denies descriptions ever refer. The analysis is compatible with a description's picking out an object when it is uniquely satisfied, and Donnellan's referential use shows that a speaker can succeed in referring even when the description misdescribes, as when a speaker says 'the man drinking a martini' about a man holding water. The second error is to think Strawson refuted Russell. The two are answering different questions: Russell offers truth conditions for sentences, Strawson offers an account of what a speaker does in using one, and a theorist can accept both by assigning the presupposition to pragmatics. The third error is to read the analysis as a psychological claim about how hearers process descriptions, which it is not; it is a claim about the structure that fixes entailments, and it can be right even if no one ever reasons in quantifier notation. A diagnostic: if you find yourself saying that Russell thought descriptions are meaningless or that Strawson showed the analysis to be false, you have strengthened one view and weakened the other beyond what either text supports.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Write down five sentences containing definite descriptions, drawn from a news report, a contract or rule, a scientific claim, a joke, and a sentence you have uttered. For each, do three things. First, paraphrase it in Russell's form, making existence and uniqueness explicit, and mark whether the uniqueness clause is doing real work or is trivially satisfied. Second, negate it twice, once with the negation outside the quantifier and once inside, and state which reading a hearer would naturally take and why. Third, decide whether the case is better described as a false assertion or as a presupposition failure, and say what turns on the choice. Model response for the scientific case: 'the cause of the outbreak was the pump' parses as there being exactly one cause, which is almost certainly false in a multifactorial outbreak, so the Russellian reading makes the claim too strong and the sensible repair is to weaken it to 'a cause' or to a contrastive claim. Self-review rubric: (1) each paraphrase is syntactically complete, with both quantifier clauses; (2) the two negation readings are distinguished by scope and not by emphasis alone; (3) the presupposition verdict is supported by a test, such as asking whether the speaker would accept 'that is false' as an adequate response; (4) at least one case is identified where the uniqueness clause makes the sentence false although ordinary speakers would call it true, since those cases are where the theory earns or loses its plausibility.
depth.summary: Russell's contribution is a technique rather than a doctrine: before assessing a sentence, ask what it logically commits you to, and be prepared for the grammatical subject to disappear in the analysis. Applied to descriptions, the technique converts apparent reference to non-existent objects into false existential claims, gives negation a scope and therefore determinate readings, and explains why identity statements with descriptions are informative without positing senses. The live disputes are about what the technique leaves out: presupposition, referential use, and the pragmatics of assertion. Lesson 103 takes up that remainder directly by asking what speakers do when they utter a sentence, rather than what the sentence means.

visual.title: Grammatical subject dissolved into a quantifier, with the two negation readings
visual.description: A diagram taking one sentence with a description through Russell's paraphrase and then splitting into the two scope readings of its negation.
steps: Input sentence: 'the F is G', with 'the F' occupying the grammatical subject position and appearing to name an object
Step one, existence: assert that at least one thing is F, which converts the apparent name into a condition that can fail
Step two, uniqueness: assert that at most one thing is F, which is what the definite article contributes
Step three, predication: assert that whatever is F is G, which carries the original predicate
Negation branch A, wide scope: 'not (there is exactly one F and it is G)', true when no F exists
Negation branch B, narrow scope: 'there is exactly one F and it is not G', false when no F exists
Contrast box: Strawson's alternative, in which 'the F' presupposes existence, so neither branch is true or false and the sentence is not assessable

lessons.title: Speech acts and implicature: saying, doing, and implying
lessons.explanation: Russell's analysis tells you what a sentence commits its user to; it does not tell you what the user is doing. Austin's William James lectures, published as 'How to Do Things with Words' (1962), begin from the observation that many utterances do not describe anything but change the world: saying 'I promise' makes a promise, saying 'I name this ship' names it, saying 'I bet' creates a bet. Austin first marked these as performatives against constatives, then abandoned the distinction because every utterance turns out to have both a content and a force. His replacement distinguishes three aspects of a single act. The locutionary act is saying something with a sense and a reference. The illocutionary act is what is done in saying it: asserting, promising, ordering, warning, christening. The perlocutionary act is what is brought about by saying it: persuading, alarming, embarrassing. The illocutionary act is governed by felicity conditions rather than by truth alone, since a promise can be sincere or insincere, authorised or unauthorised, and can fail without being false. Searle's 'Speech Acts' (1969) systematises the taxonomy into assertives, directives, commissives, expressives, and declaratives, and adds the idea of direction of fit: assertions are supposed to match the world, orders and promises are supposed to change it. Grice's 'Logic and Conversation' (1975) supplies the complementary account of how hearers recover meaning that is not said. Speakers are presumed to be cooperative, and the presumption is articulated as maxims of quantity, quality, relation, and manner. When a speaker visibly fails a maxim in a way that can be explained by the assumption that he is nevertheless cooperating, the hearer computes an implicature: an additional proposition the speaker meant but did not say.
lessons.example: A reference letter reads in full: 'The candidate's command of medieval Latin is excellent, and his attendance was regular.' The panel concludes that his philosophical work is weak, and the candidate objects that the letter says no such thing. Both are right in their own terms. Grice's apparatus explains the panel's inference. The writer has flouted the maxim of quantity by saying far less than a letter of recommendation requires, and the maxim of relation by omitting anything relevant to the post. A cooperative writer who had favourable evidence would have included it; the hearer reasons that the omission is informative, and concludes that the writer had nothing favourable to report. The resulting proposition is an implicature, not an entailment, and the tests show the difference. It is cancellable: the writer could add 'I mean to say nothing about his philosophy' without contradiction, which he could not do if the criticism were entailed. It is calculable: the hearer can reconstruct the reasoning from the maxims, which is why the inference feels rational rather than arbitrary. It is not detachable from the content in the way a conventional implication would be, since any wording conveying the same paucity of information would carry it. Contrast a case of entailment: 'the candidate has never taught a class' entails that he has no teaching experience, and no addition can cancel it without contradiction. The same distinction applies to 'some': 'some of the reports were accurate' implicates, but does not entail, that not all were, which is why 'some, and in fact all' is odd but not contradictory.
lessons.question: An email from a supplier's account manager states that 'we will look at the proposal again in the new year'. The supplier's lawyer says this is a binding commitment to reconsider; the buyer's lawyer says it commits to nothing. On Grice's account, what has been communicated and with what status?
lessons.answer: A weak commissive is implicated rather than asserted, arising from the maxims of quantity and manner, and it is cancellable, so it creates no entailment and at most a pragmatic expectation
lessons.distractor: The words assert a promise, because in a commercial context the maxim of relation makes any reference to future consideration a commitment
lessons.correction: The distractor converts a calculable implicature into an entailment and thereby ignores cancellability, which is the test that distinguishes the two. A phrase like 'will look at again' is deliberately non-committal precisely because the implicature can be retreated from; a drafter who wanted a commitment would use 'shall reconsider' and specify consequences. The learner's error is to reason from what a cooperative speaker would be taken to mean to what the sentence logically requires.

depth.definitions: A locutionary act is the utterance of a sentence with a determinate sense and reference. An illocutionary act is the act performed in uttering it, identified by its force: assertion, request, promise, warning, declaration. A perlocutionary act is the production of an effect by means of the utterance, such as persuading or deterring. Felicity conditions are the conditions an illocutionary act must satisfy to be successfully performed: the speaker must have the relevant standing, the procedure must be executed correctly and completely, and the accompanying thoughts and intentions must be appropriate. A constative is an utterance that says something true or false; a performative is one that does something, in Austin's early terminology. An implicature is a proposition communicated by an utterance without being entailed by it; a conversational implicature depends on the maxims and the context, while a conventional implicature attaches to particular words such as 'but' or 'therefore'. The cooperative principle is the presumption that speakers contribute what is required, at the stage required, for the accepted purpose of the exchange.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms are at work and they should be kept apart. The first is conventional: certain utterances count as acts because a practice or institution assigns them that role, as Searle puts it, 'X counts as Y in context C'. On that account the illocutionary force of a declaration is constituted by a rule, which is why a person without standing can utter the words and produce no declaration at all. The second is inferential: implicatures are derived by the hearer's reasoning from the said content, the presumption of cooperation, and the observable fact that a maxim has been flouted. Grice's criterion is calculability, the availability of that reasoning as an explanation of how the hearer arrived at the further proposition. Both mechanisms explain why force is not a matter of the words alone, but they differ in what they predict. If force were conventional, a mismatch between words and standing would make the act void; if force were purely inferential, a hearer's recognition of intention would be sufficient. Austin's felicity conditions and Searle's constitutive rules place the weight on the first mechanism, while Grice places it on the second, and many disputes about hate speech, consent, and contractual formation turn on which mechanism is doing the work.
depth.secondExample: A departmental administrator emails 'I approve this expenditure' for a purchase that exceeds her delegated authority. Three questions can be asked, and the vocabulary separates them. Did she perform a locutionary act? Yes: the sentence has a sense and a reference, and it is perfectly intelligible. Did she perform the illocutionary act of approving? No, because approval requires standing, and standing is a felicity condition rather than a feature of the words, so the act misfires even though nothing in the sentence is false. Did she perform a perlocutionary act? Very likely: the supplier may read the email and begin work, and the effect is real even though the act that was supposed to produce it was void. The case shows why the threefold distinction earns its keep, because a single utterance can succeed at one level and fail at another, and the failure is neither a falsehood nor a misunderstanding. It also shows the practical stakes: an organisation that treats the perlocutionary effect as evidence of the illocutionary act will believe it has approved things it never approved, which is the administrative analogue of mistaking a threat for a prediction.
depth.mistake: Three errors are common. The first is to think Austin held that all utterances are performatives. He introduced the constative/performative distinction, found counterexamples to it, and replaced it with the locutionary/illocutionary/perlocutionary analysis precisely because the earlier contrast collapsed. The second is to treat an implicature as part of what was said, which makes the speaker's implication inescapable and turns cancellability into inconsistency. The opposite error is equally damaging: because implicatures are cancellable, a speaker may conclude that nothing was communicated beyond the literal words, which ignores that hearers reasonably rely on implicatures and that some of them are as binding socially as assertions. The third is to identify the illocutionary act with its perlocutionary effect, so that a warning counts as successful only if it frightens someone, or a request counts as made only if it is obeyed. Diagnostics: ask of any disputed utterance what was said, what was done in saying it, and what followed from saying it, and refuse to let an answer at one level settle a question at another.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Collect four utterances from your own week: one email, one utterance in a meeting, one advertisement, and one sentence from a contract or rule. For each, complete a five-line entry. Line one, the locution: paraphrase the content without adding anything. Line two, the force: name the illocutionary act and give the feature of the context that supports the classification, such as the speaker's standing or the presence of an undertaking. Line three, the perlocutionary effect: state what actually followed. Line four, any implicature: state it, name the maxim that generated it, and write a cancellation that would defeat it. Line five, a felicity audit: list which conditions were satisfied and which were not. Model response for an advertisement reading 'now with 30 per cent more fibre': locution, the product contains 30 per cent more fibre than before; force, an assertive in a persuasive context, with an implicature that the increase is nutritionally significant; perlocution, purchase; felicity, the assertion is assessable but the comparison class is unstated, which is a manner problem rather than a falsehood. Self-review rubric: (1) the locution paraphrase contains no evaluative language; (2) the force is supported by context rather than by the sentence's mood alone; (3) at least one cancellation is actually written out; (4) no verdict about truth is offered for a question that is about force.
depth.summary: Meaning is layered. A sentence has a content, an utterance of it has a force, and the utterance has effects; and beyond the content there are implicatures that a hearer is entitled to recover though the speaker has not asserted them. The transferable discipline is diagnostic: separate what was said, what was done, and what followed, and then ask which of these a dispute is really about. Most disputes that look like disagreements about meaning are disagreements about force, standing, or the reliability of an implicature, and treating them as disagreements about truth conditions makes them unresolvable. Lesson 104 returns to names and asks whether the descriptive content that Frege and Russell assigned to them is content at all.

lessons.title: Rigid designation and the necessary a posteriori: Kripke against descriptivism
lessons.explanation: The descriptivist tradition, running from Frege and Russell through Searle, holds that the meaning of a proper name is given by a description the speaker associates with it: 'Aristotle' means something like 'the student of Plato who taught Alexander'. Kripke's 'Naming and Necessity' (lectures of 1970, published 1980) attacks the thesis with a modal argument and then draws a distinction that reorganises the whole subject. A rigid designator is an expression that designates the same object in every possible world in which that object exists; a non-rigid designator designates different objects in different worlds. 'The teacher of Alexander' is non-rigid, since in another world someone else, or no one, teaches Alexander. 'Aristotle' is rigid: when we consider a world in which Aristotle took up zoology, we are considering a world about him, not about whoever happens to have taught Alexander there. From this follow the modal argument, the observation that identity statements between rigid designators are necessary if true, and the diagnosis of a deep confusion between two kinds of modality. A proposition is necessary when it could not have been false, and a priori when it can be known without experience. These are different properties, and Kripke shows that they come apart. 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' is necessary, because the two names designate one object and an object is identical with itself in every world, yet it was known only a posteriori. The standard metre bar is one metre long at the moment of stipulation, which is knowable a priori yet contingent, since the bar could have been longer.
lessons.example: Take the name 'Aristotle' and the description 'the teacher of Alexander'. If the description gave the name's meaning, then 'Aristotle might not have taught Alexander' would mean 'the teacher of Alexander might not have taught Alexander', which is self-contradictory in the way that 'the bachelor might not have been unmarried' is. But the modal claim is true: Aristotle might have spent his life on marine biology and never met Alexander. Since the premise of the descriptivist analysis yields a false prediction about a true modal claim, the analysis is wrong. The argument is not merely about Aristotle; it generalises to any name and any description that the speaker associates with it, which is why Kripke can conclude that no description supplies the meaning of a name. Now consider two replies and their costs. The first is that the description should be rigidified: 'Aristotle' means 'the person who actually taught Alexander'. Kripke's objection is that this rescues the modal claim at the price of triviality, because the actuality operator makes the description a rigid designator whose reference is fixed by the actual world, and any name at all could be given a meaning of that form. The second reply, developed by Dummett and by Jackson, is that the descriptivist should distinguish the description that fixes the reference from the description that gives the sense, and locate the a priori element in the former. Kripke allows a version of this: a description can fix the reference of a name without being synonymous with it, as when a speaker introduces 'Jack the Ripper' as 'whoever committed those murders'. The distinction between reference-fixing and meaning is one of the lesson's main products.
lessons.question: A historian argues that because we can imagine Aristotle never teaching Alexander, 'Aristotle' cannot mean 'the teacher of Alexander'. A colleague replies that the modal claim is irrelevant: what we can imagine is a fact about us, not about the name. Who has the better of the argument, and why?
lessons.answer: The historian does: if the description were the name's meaning, the modal claim would be false by substitution, and since it is true the description cannot be the meaning, which is a point about designation and not about our imaginative powers
lessons.distractor: The colleague does: conceivability is psychological, so no conclusion about meaning follows, and the descriptivist analysis stands until a semantic counterexample is produced
lessons.correction: The colleague misidentifies what the modal claim is doing. The argument does not infer possibility from imaginability; it takes the truth of the counterfactual as a datum about how the name behaves across worlds, and shows that the descriptivist substitution yields a falsehood. The learner's error is to hear a conceivability premise where the argument contains a premise about designation, which makes a strong argument look like a weak one.

depth.definitions: A rigid designator designates the same object with respect to every possible world, and in particular with respect to the actual world; a non-rigid or accidental designator may designate different objects at different worlds. A proper name is the standard case of rigidity, and natural kind terms such as 'water' and 'gold' are widely held to be rigid too. De dicto modality attaches to a sentence or proposition, as in 'it is necessary that eight is greater than seven'; de re modality attaches to an object, as in 'eight is necessarily greater than seven'. A proposition is a posteriori if it can be known only through experience, and a priori if it can be known independently of experience; these are epistemic categories, whereas necessity and contingency are metaphysical ones. Essence is the set of properties an object could not lack, and essentialism is the thesis that objects have such properties independently of how we describe them. A causal-historical chain of reference is the picture on which a name is introduced at a baptism and transmitted through a community, with later speakers borrowing the reference rather than describing the object.
depth.mechanism: The argument works by substitution into a modal context. If a name is synonymous with a description, then in any sentence the name can be replaced by the description without change of meaning, including sentences governed by 'possibly' and 'necessarily'. The resulting sentence has a different truth value from the original, so the synonymy thesis is false. What fills the gap is rigidity: a name refers to the same individual at every world, while a description picks out whatever satisfies it at each world, so the two expressions behave differently under modal operators even when they pick out the same object in the actual world. The necessity of true identities follows from the same machinery, since if a and b are the same object, then at every world where a exists, a is that object, and b is that object too. The epistemic contrast is explained by the route of access: the proposition is necessary in virtue of the identity of the objects, but our route to knowing which objects are identical can be empirical, since the names may reach the object through different causal chains that we must investigate. This separation of the metaphysical question (could it have been otherwise) from the epistemic question (how could we know) is the lesson's central instrument, and it recurs in lessons 105, 106, and 110.
depth.secondExample: Consider 'water is H2O'. Before chemistry, speakers used 'water' competently while believing that water was a fundamental element. If the term's meaning were the description speakers associated with it, the chemical identification would be a change of subject rather than a discovery. On Kripke's and Putnam's account, 'water' is a rigid designator for a natural kind, and the identity with H2O, once established, is necessary: there is no possible world in which this substance, water, has a different chemical constitution, though there are worlds containing a different substance that resembles water and that we might have called by the same name. The proposition is therefore necessary and a posteriori, which the Frege-Russell framework could not accommodate, since necessity was tied to analyticity and thus to a priority. Kripke applies the same pattern to theoretical identities in the philosophy of mind: if pain were identical with a brain state, the identity would be necessary, and since it seems conceivable that pain occur without that state, either the identity is false or the conceivability intuition is unreliable in a way that needs independent support. That argument is contested, and its critics reply that the appearance of contingency for identities involving phenomenal states reflects an epistemic gap rather than a metaphysical one; the point for this lesson is that the framework makes the dispute precise instead of settling it.
depth.mistake: The first error is to treat necessity and a priority as the same property, which makes 'necessary a posteriori' sound like a contradiction. They answer different questions: whether the proposition could have been false, and how it can be known. The second is to conclude that rigidity implies names have no descriptive content at all. Kripke explicitly allows that a description may fix a reference, as a speaker may introduce a name by pointing to the person who discovered the theorem; what he denies is that the description is synonymous with the name and therefore that it survives substitution in modal contexts. The third is to think the modal argument refutes Frege's sense. It refutes a specific thesis, descriptivism about names, and Frege's modes of presentation need not be descriptive in the required sense, which is why two-dimensionalist accounts can accept Kripke's cases while retaining a version of the Fregean picture. A diagnostic: whenever you are tempted to say that Kripke showed names have no meaning, ask whether the claim is about reference, about cognitive significance, or about essence, because the argument bears on these differently.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose three names, one of a person, one of a place, and one of a chemical or biological kind. For each, write four lines. Line one, the descriptive content you associate with the term, stated as a definite description. Line two, the modal test: construct a sentence of the form 'X might not have been the F', substituting the description for the name, and record whether it is true. Line three, an identity statement involving the term, and a verdict on whether it is necessary, contingent, a priori, or a posteriori, with a defence of each label. Line four, a note on whether the description is doing the work of fixing the reference or of giving the meaning, and what difference that makes to the argument. Model response for a place name: 'Everest' is associated with 'the highest mountain'; 'Everest might not have been the highest mountain' is true, which refutes the synonymy thesis; 'Everest is the highest mountain' is contingent and a posteriori, while 'Everest is Everest' is necessary; the description fixes the reference without giving the meaning. Self-review rubric: (1) the modal sentence is grammatical and its truth value is argued for rather than asserted; (2) necessity and a priority are labelled separately for each statement; (3) at least one description is correctly classified as reference-fixing; (4) no claim is made about what speakers believe unless it is supported by evidence about actual usage.
depth.summary: Kripke's contribution is a distinction between two ways an expression can attach to the world, and between two ways a truth can be necessary. Names and kind terms are rigid, so they carry the object across worlds; descriptions are not, so substituting one for a name changes what is said about other worlds. Once this is seen, the necessary a posteriori stops being paradoxical and becomes the normal case for identities discovered by science. The cost is that the Fregean identification of meaning with cognitive route has to be given up or relocated, and lesson 105 takes up that cost by asking whether the reference of a kind term can be fixed by anything inside the speaker's head.

lessons.title: Natural kind terms and semantic externalism: Twin Earth and the division of linguistic labour
lessons.explanation: Lesson 104 left names attached to their objects by a causal chain rather than by a description in the speaker's mind. Putnam's 'The Meaning of "Meaning"' (1975) pushes the same idea into general terms for kinds of stuff and shows that it has consequences for what philosophy can discover from the armchair. The argument is a twin case. Suppose there is a planet, Twin Earth, where the clear, drinkable, thirst-quenching liquid is not H2O but a different compound, abbreviated XYZ, which behaves like water at ordinary temperatures and pressures. Oscar on Earth and Twin Oscar on Twin Earth are molecule-for-molecule identical, have identical histories, and are having identical experiences. When each says 'water quenches thirst', the word in Oscar's mouth refers to H2O and the word in Twin Oscar's mouth refers to XYZ, so the sentences express different propositions and the terms differ in meaning. Since the speakers' internal states are the same, meaning cannot be fixed by internal state alone. Putnam's summary is that meanings just are not in the head. Two further elements complete the picture. The extension of a kind term is the set of things it applies to, while the stereotype is the body of beliefs ordinary speakers associate with it, and the two can diverge sharply. And reference is often fixed through a division of linguistic labour, in which most speakers defer to a subgroup of experts who can discriminate the kind, which is why a competent speaker can use 'elm' correctly while being unable to tell an elm from a beech.
lessons.example: Putnam's own version sets the case in 1750, before either community has any chemistry. Oscar and Twin Oscar in that year have identical beliefs about the liquid, including the belief that it is an element, and neither could distinguish H2O from XYZ by any test available to them. Nevertheless, Putnam argues, the extension of 'water' differed in the two communities, because the term was answering to a different substance. This is the strongest form of the argument, since it does not rely on what the speakers know, only on what their words are answerable to. A natural objection is that in 1750 no one could have meant anything different, because the difference was undetectable in principle for them. Putnam's reply is that the reference of a kind term is not exhausted by what speakers can detect; a term introduced to talk about the stuff in the rivers and lakes inherits whatever underlying nature that stuff has, and the nature is a fact about the world rather than a fact about the speakers' evidence. The argument is not that Oscar and Twin Oscar mean different things because they are in different places, which would be trivial; it is that a complete inventory of what is inside their heads leaves out a determinant of meaning, so no amount of internal description can settle what their words refer to. That is the precise sense in which meaning is external.
lessons.question: A philosopher concludes that because Oscar and Twin Oscar are molecule-for-molecule identical, their words mean the same and the difference between them lies only in their surroundings. Which premise of Putnam's argument does this conclusion deny, and what follows?
lessons.answer: It denies that the extension of a term is part of its meaning and therefore that meaning varies with the kind a term is answerable to; once extension is counted, the twins' words differ in meaning although their narrow content is shared
lessons.distractor: It denies nothing, because if the twins' internal states are identical then whatever varies between them must be external, which is exactly what externalism says
lessons.correction: The distractor mistakes the conclusion for a restatement of the premise. Externalism says that meaning itself varies with the environment, not that meaning is constant while surroundings vary; the whole point is that the difference in environment shows up as a difference in what the words mean. The learner's error is to preserve an individualist reading of meaning while accepting externalist-sounding language about surroundings.

depth.definitions: The extension of a general term is the set of things to which it correctly applies. The stereotype is the cluster of properties ordinary speakers associate with the term, such as being clear, odourless, and drinkable, and it guides recognition without determining extension. Semantic externalism is the thesis that the meaning or content of at least some expressions is partly determined by factors outside the speaker's body; semantic internalism denies this. Narrow content is the component of content that supervenes on internal physical states, and wide content is content that does not. The division of linguistic labour is the arrangement by which reference is transmitted through experts, so that a speaker's term inherits an extension fixed by others. Content externalism is the corresponding thesis about thoughts rather than words, and it is the target of Burge's arthritis example. Supervenience is the relation in which one family of facts is fixed by another, so that there can be no difference in the first without a difference in the second; the twin arguments are arguments against the supervenience of content on internal states.
depth.mechanism: The argument has a single elegant form. Assume that content supervenes on internal physical states. Then any two subjects with identical internal states have identical content. Oscar and Twin Oscar have identical internal states. Therefore they have identical content. But their terms differ in extension, and difference in extension is a difference in meaning for a kind term. Contradiction. Therefore content does not supervene on internal states. The conclusion is modal rather than empirical: it concerns what is possible for physically identical subjects, not what is actual. Burge's variant changes the external factor from the physical environment to the social one, which is why the two arguments are usually presented together. His patient believes he has arthritis in his thigh; in his community 'arthritis' applies only to joints, so the belief is false and its content is about a joint disease misapplied. In a community where the word covers thigh ailments, an internally identical patient has a true belief with a different content. The pair shows that the same internal state can realise different thoughts, so the social environment is as much a determinant of content as the chemical one. It is worth noting what the argument does not require: it does not require that speakers be able to detect the difference, and it does not require that any particular theory of reference be true, only that extension is determined by something other than the speaker's concepts.
depth.secondExample: Consider a legal rather than a chemical kind: 'burglary'. In one jurisdiction the offence requires entry as a trespasser with intent to commit a listed offence; in another the statute omits the trespass requirement and covers entry by deception. Two lawyers with identical training, vocabulary, and internal states use the word 'burglary' in their respective courts, and their sentences about what counts as burglary diverge. The divergence is not a disagreement about concepts, since each is applying the local rule correctly, and it is not a difference in narrow content, since the lawyers could be molecule-for-molecule identical. It is a difference in extension produced by an institution. The case is useful because it separates externalism from any commitment to chemical essences: what fixes the extension here is a statute, and the mechanism of deference is the same one that operates for 'elm' and 'water'. It also disciplines an overstatement. Putnam sometimes writes as though the world alone fixes reference, but institutional kinds show that the relevant external factor can be a convention, which means externalism is a family of theses about what determines extension rather than a single doctrine about nature.
depth.mistake: The first error is to think externalism claims that meanings are objects in the world, like parcels; the thesis concerns what determines meaning, not what meaning is. The second is to think externalism entails that 'water' means H2O. It entails that the term refers to whatever the actual kind is, which chemists may discover, but the meaning is not the formula, and the term would have referred to XYZ had the actual kind been XYZ. The third is to conclude that introspection is worthless. The standard compatibilist reply distinguishes a priori knowledge of narrow content from knowledge of wide content, so a subject can know how things seem while being ignorant of what her terms refer to, and the slow-switching cases are designed to test exactly that boundary. The fourth, and the one that matters most for this level, is to think that because meaning is external, conceptual analysis is impossible. What follows is narrower: armchair analysis can articulate stereotypes and inferential roles, but it cannot deliver essences, which is why the method of lesson 110 has to be argued for rather than assumed.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Construct two twin cases of your own, one for a natural kind and one for an institutional or artefactual kind, and write each as a four-part argument. Part one, describe the actual case and the twin case so that the subjects are internally identical and only the external factor varies. Part two, state the extension of the term in each case and justify it without appealing to what the subjects believe. Part three, run the supervenience argument explicitly, naming the assumption, the twin premise, the extension premise, and the contradiction. Part four, identify one objection and answer it or concede it. Model response for the institutional case: the actual jurisdiction criminalises entry by deception and the twin does not; the extension of 'burglary' differs although the lawyers are internally identical; the supervenience of content on internal states is refuted for this term; the objection that institutional kinds are stipulated rather than discovered is answered by noting that the stipulation is itself the external determinant, which is all the argument needs. Self-review rubric: (1) the subjects really are internally identical, with no smuggled difference in belief; (2) extension is justified by a fact about the world or the institution, not by majority usage; (3) the argument's form is displayed rather than gestured at; (4) the objection is stated in its strongest form and not as a straw position.
depth.summary: Meaning is not exhausted by what is inside a speaker's head. The twin cases establish this by holding the inside fixed and varying the outside, and the division of linguistic labour explains how ordinary speakers can use terms whose extension they cannot themselves determine. The consequence for method is significant: if extension is fixed partly by the world or by institutions, then conceptual analysis can describe our concepts but cannot by itself establish what those concepts answer to, and the discovery of essences becomes an empirical matter. That conclusion sets up the second unit, which asks what kind of necessity such discoveries involve and whether the disputes of metaphysics are discoveries about the world or decisions about which framework to use.

visual.description: A diagram comparing Earth and Twin Earth with the same internal states and different extensions, leading to the failure of supervenience and the division-of-labour route.

questions.prompt: A newspaper profile states that Lois believes Superman can fly, and the same issue reports that Superman is Clark Kent. A subeditor concludes that Lois believes Clark Kent can fly, and is surprised when the sentence reads as false. Using Frege's distinction, what has gone wrong, and what does it show about the names inside the belief report?
questions.answer: The two names share a reference but differ in sense, and inside the report the words stand for their customary senses rather than for the man, so the substitution changes the thought attributed and the conclusion does not follow
questions.distractor: Identity is not substitutable in any context, so Leibniz's law fails generally and no term may ever be replaced by a co-referential one
questions.correction: Substitution works wherever a term stands for its ordinary reference, as in 'Superman is Clark Kent, and Superman can fly, so Clark Kent can fly'; the failure is confined to intensional contexts, where on Frege's account the terms refer to their senses. The distractor over-generalises a local exception into the collapse of the law of identity, which would make ordinary reasoning about identities impossible rather than merely context-sensitive.

questions.prompt: A minute records: 'The chair of the safety committee approved the override.' The committee had been dissolved a month earlier and had no chair. A member argues that because the description has no referent, both the minute's sentence and its negation are neither true nor false, so no finding of fault can be recorded. Is that reasoning sound?
questions.answer: No: on Russell's analysis the sentence is false and its wide-scope negation true, so there is no truth-value gap, and avoiding both meaninglessness and gaps was the point of the theory of descriptions
questions.distractor: Yes: a description that fails to denote makes the sentence meaningless, and a meaningless sentence cannot ground any finding
questions.correction: Strawson's account yields failure of presupposition, not meaninglessness, and Russell's analysis was constructed precisely to keep such sentences assessable. The learner's error is to accept Strawson's conclusion as common ground and then to inflate 'neither true nor false' into 'meaningless', which strengthens the position under criticism into something neither philosopher held.

questions.prompt: A reference letter reads in full: 'The candidate's command of medieval Latin is excellent, and his attendance was regular.' The hiring panel concludes that his philosophical work is weak. The candidate protests that the letter contains no such statement. Who is right about what the letter says, and on what does the panel's inference rest?
questions.answer: The candidate is right that nothing of the kind is asserted, and the panel's conclusion is a conversational implicature generated by flouting the maxims of quantity and relation, hence cancellable and not part of what is said
questions.distractor: The panel is right that the letter asserts the candidate is weak, since a maxim of relevance makes whatever a cooperative writer omits part of the letter's literal content
questions.correction: Implicature is calculated from what is said together with the assumption of cooperation, and it can be cancelled without contradiction ('his Latin is excellent, though I mean to say nothing about his philosophy'), which is the test separating it from entailment. The distractor turns a pragmatic inference into a truth condition and so makes the letter assert something its author could deny without inconsistency.

questions.prompt: A historian objects to the thesis that names are abbreviated descriptions: 'If Aristotle meant the teacher of Alexander, then the statement that Aristotle might not have taught Alexander would be false. But it is true, since he might have devoted himself to zoology. So the description is not the meaning of the name.' Reconstruct the argument and state what it establishes.
questions.answer: The argument is valid: a description supplies only a contingent property, so if it were the name's meaning the modal claim would be false, and since the modal claim is true the name designates the man rigidly in every world where he exists
questions.distractor: The argument fails because the premise that Aristotle might not have taught Alexander is false, since he did teach Alexander and possibility cannot outrun actuality
questions.correction: The distractor reads a modal claim as a claim about actual history, which is exactly the confusion the argument is designed to expose. Note also what the conclusion does not establish: it is about designation, not about whether speakers associate descriptions with names, which Kripke allows as a way of fixing the reference without giving the name's meaning.

questions.prompt: Oscar on Earth and Twin Oscar on Twin Earth are molecule-for-molecule identical. Each says 'water is wet' of the clear liquid around him, which is H2O on Earth and XYZ on Twin Earth. A philosopher concludes that because their inner states are identical their words mean the same, and the difference lies only in their surroundings. Assess that conclusion.
questions.answer: It is false as stated: the terms differ in extension and therefore in meaning, so meaning is not fixed by internal state alone, and identity of inner state yields at most identity of narrow content
questions.distractor: It is true, because meaning is a psychological state, and two subjects in identical psychological states cannot mean different things by the same word
questions.correction: The distractor states the individualist premise the experiment is designed to refute rather than a consequence of it. It also slides from 'narrow content is shared' to 'meaning is shared', which begs the question; externalism permits a shared narrow component while denying that the component exhausts meaning.

units.title: Necessity, time, composition, and the revision of concepts

lessons.title: Possible worlds: what modal claims quantify over, and what each account costs
lessons.explanation: Lesson 104 established that identity statements between rigid designators are necessary if true, and that names carry their objects across worlds. That leaves the central question untouched: what is a possible world, such that a claim about one can be true? Leibniz's answer, in the 'Theodicy' (1710), was that possible worlds are ideas in the divine understanding, ranked by goodness. Contemporary metaphysics secularises the idea into three families. Concretism, defended by Lewis in 'On the Plurality of Worlds' (1986), holds that possible worlds are concrete universes as real as the actual one, spatiotemporally isolated from it, and that 'actual' is an indexical term like 'here', picking out the world of the speaker. Abstractionism, or ersatzism, holds that worlds are abstract entities, either maximal consistent propositions or maximal states of affairs, as in Plantinga's 'The Nature of Necessity' (1974) and Stalnaker's 'Possible Worlds' (1976). Combinatorialism, associated with Armstrong's 'A Combinatorial Theory of Possibility' (1989), holds that worlds are recombinations of the actual world's particulars, properties, and relations. Each account buys the same logical service at a different price. The service is a semantics for modal operators: 'possibly P' is true when some world is one in which P, and 'necessarily P' when every world is. The price is a combination of ontological commitment and ideological primitiveness: concretism pays in entities and avoids primitive modality, ersatzism pays in primitive modality and avoids entities, combinatorialism pays with difficulties about necessary connections between distinct existences.
lessons.example: Take the claim 'Humphrey might have won the 1968 election', where in fact he lost. On a transworld-identity account, there is a world in which Humphrey himself wins, and the modal claim is about that very man at another world. Lewis rejects transworld identity as unintelligible without haecceities, properties of being identical with a particular individual, which he regards as unacceptably mysterious. His counterpart theory replaces it: Humphrey does not exist at other worlds, but he has counterparts there, individuals who resemble him closely and who occupy his role in the local history, and the modal claim says that some counterpart of Humphrey wins. The difference is not merely terminological. Transworld identity makes modal properties intrinsic to the individual; counterpart theory makes them relational, since whether Humphrey could have won depends on the resemblance relations between him and other-worldly individuals. Lewis accepts that cost, arguing that it is the price of avoiding bare haecceities and that it explains why we count worlds by resemblance rather than by a special transworld identity relation. The case therefore displays the general shape of the debate: the same modal sentence gets truth conditions under every account, and the argument turns on which theoretical virtues, parsimony of entities, parsimony of primitives, and fidelity to ordinary modal judgement, are ranked how.
lessons.question: An essay argues: 'There is a possible world in which you have a sister. So you have a sister in that world, and therefore a sister exists.' A critic says the conclusion does not follow, while a modal realist insists that all worlds are as concrete as ours. Who is right, and on what does the inference turn?
lessons.answer: The critic is right: the quantifier over worlds is restricted, and existence at a world is not existence in the actual world, so even on concretism the sister is not among the things here
lessons.distractor: The modal realist is right, because if all worlds are equally concrete then whatever exists at any world exists without qualification and actuality is a mere honorific
lessons.correction: Concretism is a thesis about what worlds are, not about what exists here; Lewis pairs it with counterpart theory and an indexical analysis of actuality precisely so that 'possibly a sister exists' does not entail that a sister exists. The distractor conflates existence at a world with existence simpliciter, which is the restriction the quantifier exists to enforce, and it would make modal realism entail that everything possible is actual, which is the opposite of the view.

depth.definitions: A possible world is a way things might have been, treated as an entity over which modal operators quantify. The actual world is the way things are. Concretism is the thesis that worlds are concrete totalities of the same kind as the actual universe; abstractionism is the thesis that they are abstract representations, such as maximal consistent propositions or maximal states of affairs; combinatorialism is the thesis that they are recombinations of actual elements. De dicto modality attaches to a sentence or proposition, as in 'it is necessary that there are no married bachelors'; de re modality attaches to an object, as in 'this table is necessarily made of wood'. A counterpart relation is a relation of similarity between individuals at different worlds, used instead of transworld identity. An essence is a property an object has necessarily and that is explanatory of what the object is, and the relation between essence and necessity is the live issue in section 3 of the entry named below. Accessibility is the relation between worlds that restricts which worlds are relevant to a modal operator in quantified modal logic.
depth.mechanism: The semantics works by treating modal operators as quantifiers over indices. A model consists of a set of worlds, an accessibility relation, and a valuation assigning extensions to predicates at each world. 'Possibly P' is true at a world when P is true at some world accessible from it; 'Necessarily P' when P is true at every accessible world. This machinery is neutral between the three conceptions, which is why the metaphysics can be debated separately from the logic. What is not neutral is the treatment of de re claims. To say that an object has a property necessarily, the semantics needs a way of identifying the object across worlds. Transworld identity supplies that directly, at the cost of an identity relation that holds between an object and itself at different worlds. Counterpart theory supplies it indirectly, through resemblance, at the cost of making modal properties relational. Ersatzism supplies it through the content of the representing proposition, at the cost of taking representation and consistency as primitive. Each move is a different answer to the same question, how a claim can be about a particular thing at a world where that thing may not exist, and the debate is best understood as a comparison of those answers rather than as a dispute about whether modal talk is legitimate.
depth.secondExample: Fine's 'Essence and Modality' (1994) argues that necessity and essence come apart, which constrains any account of de re modality built on worlds alone. It is necessary that the number 2 is a member of the singleton containing 2, since in every world the set exists and contains its member. Yet it is not essential to 2 that it belong to that set: the membership holds because the set depends on the number, not because the number depends on the set, and it would be a strange inversion to say that what 2 is includes being collected into a set by someone. Fine concludes that essentialist truths cannot be defined as necessary truths about an object, and that essence must be taken as primitive, with modality derivative from it rather than the reverse. The argument matters here because it shows the limits of the possible-worlds framework: worlds give an elegant semantics for necessity, but they do not by themselves tell you what belongs to a thing's nature. Two consequences follow. A metaphysics of modality that only quantifies over worlds is incomplete, and a metaphysics of essence needs an account of what makes a property explanatory of an object, which is a different question from whether the property holds in all worlds. The dispute is live: modal essentialists deny Fine's intuition about the singleton, and the exchange is a good test of whether one treats intuitions about explanation as data or as relics of a pre-theoretical picture.
depth.mistake: The most common error is to read 'possible world' as a distant place, so that modal claims become geographical claims about inaccessible regions. That reading makes the semantics unintelligible, since no spatiotemporal relation could make a counterfactual true or false. A second error is the opposite reduction: treating worlds as useful fictions, so that modal claims are really claims about what we can imagine. Lewis called the first response to his view the incredulous stare, and the fiction view avoids the stare by giving up the explanatory ambitions of modality, since it cannot say why the necessities hold. A third error is to confuse de dicto and de re claims, inferring from 'necessarily, whatever is F is G' to 'this F is essentially G', which is invalid whenever the description is non-rigid. A fourth is to think that accepting possible worlds commits one to Lewis's concretism, when the majority of users of the framework are abstractionists. Diagnostics: whenever a modal claim is at issue, ask whether the necessity is attached to a proposition or to an object, and ask which conception of worlds the argument needs, since many arguments that appear to require concretism need only the semantics.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose one de dicto and one de re modal claim, for instance 'there could have been no universities' and 'this university could have been founded a decade earlier'. For each, write three sections. Section one, the truth conditions under the quantifier semantics, stated formally with the quantifier, the world variable, and the condition on satisfaction. Section two, the same truth conditions under two of the three conceptions, noting where the accounts differ in what has to exist. Section three, a cost table with three rows, ontological commitment, ideological primitives, and fidelity to ordinary modal judgement, and one sentence of verdict per row. Model response for the de re claim: the semantics quantifies over worlds in which the university exists and is founded earlier, which requires an identification of the university across worlds; transworld identity supplies it directly, counterpart theory supplies it by resemblance, and the cost table shows concretism saving on primitives while paying in entities. Self-review rubric: (1) the formal statement contains an explicit quantifier and an explicit restriction to accessible worlds; (2) de dicto and de re are distinguished in the first sentence and kept distinct throughout; (3) the cost table names a specific argument rather than a general impression; (4) no claim is made about what is imaginable unless it is tied to a world and a truth condition.
depth.summary: Possible worlds are a technique for turning modal claims into quantifications, and the metaphysics of worlds is the price list attached to that technique. What survives across the three conceptions is the logical core: necessity is truth at all accessible worlds, possibility is truth at some. What varies is what has to exist for that to be so, and the arguments between concretists, ersatzists, and combinatorialists are arguments about which price is worth paying. Fine's objection adds a constraint that no account of worlds supplies on its own: essence is not the same as necessary property, so a theory of what things are cannot be read off a theory of what must be. Lesson 107 applies the same comparative method to a relation that looks simpler and turns out not to be, namely causation.

Concretism route: worlds are concrete universes, so the quantifier ranges over real objects; cost, an enormous ontology; gain, no primitive modality
Abstractionism route: worlds are maximal propositions or states of affairs; cost, primitive representation and consistency; gain, no extra concrete universes
