lessons.title: What causation is: regularity, counterfactual dependence, and intervention
lessons.explanation: Lesson 98 established that a probabilistic association does not by itself license a causal conclusion, and that confounding, selection, and reverse causation have to be ruled out. That was a lesson about inference. This lesson asks a different question: what is the relation that the inference is trying to reach? Hume's answer, in section VII of the 'Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding' (1748), is that we observe only conjunction, contiguity, and succession, and that the impression of necessary connection is a feeling produced in the mind by habit; the metaphysical content of 'cause' is exhausted by regular succession. The regularity tradition develops this into Mill's methods and into Mackie's analysis of causes as INUS conditions, insufficient but necessary parts of conditions that are themselves unnecessary but sufficient. Lewis's 'Causation' (1973) replaces regularity with counterfactual dependence: an event c causes an event e when, had c not occurred, e would not have occurred. Woodward's interventionist account, in 'Making Things Happen' (2003), and Pearl's structural-equation framework recast the counterfactual in terms of what would happen under a surgical intervention on a variable, holding the rest of the system fixed. The accounts are not merely verbal variants. They disagree about which cases are causal, they place different demands on evidence, and they answer different questions: regularity asks what patterns obtain, counterfactual accounts ask what would have happened otherwise, and interventionism asks what would change if we manipulated something.
lessons.example: Suzy throws a rock that shatters a bottle. Billy also throws, and his rock would have shattered the bottle had Suzy's missed, but it arrives a fraction of a second later. The simple counterfactual theory delivers the wrong verdict: had Suzy not thrown, the bottle would still have shattered, so by that theory Suzy's throw is not a cause, which is absurd. The case is a preemption problem, and it shows that counterfactual dependence is sufficient for causation in easy cases but not necessary. Lewis's response in the postscripts to 'Causation' was to refine the analysis, first by requiring a chain of counterfactual dependence through intermediate events, and later, in 'Causation as Influence', by requiring that the cause make a difference to the manner or timing of the effect, not only to its occurrence. Note that the refinement is not an ad hoc patch: it identifies what the preemption case actually shows, namely that Suzy's throw influences the shattering in a way that Billy's does not, even though both are sufficient. An interventionist states the same point differently. Intervening to prevent Suzy's throw, with Billy's throw held fixed, changes the time at which the bottle breaks, so the throw makes a difference to an outcome variable that includes timing. The comparison is instructive because it shows how much work the choice of variables does: whether Suzy counts as a cause depends on how finely the effect is described, which is a feature of the model rather than of the world.
lessons.question: A lawyer argues that Suzy did not cause the bottle to shatter, since had she not thrown, Billy's rock would have shattered it anyway. Assess the argument and state what it shows about the counterfactual theory of causation.
lessons.answer: The premise is true but the conclusion is false, since Suzy's throw is a cause; this shows that counterfactual dependence is not necessary for causation, so the theory must be refined rather than applied mechanically
lessons.distractor: The argument is sound, because causation just is counterfactual dependence, and where the effect would have occurred anyway there is no causation
lessons.correction: The distractor accepts the theory's verdict instead of testing the theory against a case the theory was formulated to handle; this is the standard preemption counterexample. The practical cost is visible: the reasoning would exonerate the actual producer whenever a redundant backup exists, which inverts the purpose of a causal inquiry, and it would make causation depend on the existence of backups rather than on what happened.

depth.definitions: A cause is an event or state that brings about, or contributes to bringing about, another event or state. Regularity theories identify causation with instantiations of lawful regularities, so that c causes e when events of c's type are constantly conjoined with events of e's type under the relevant conditions. An INUS condition is an insufficient but non-redundant part of an unnecessary but sufficient condition, which is Mackie's analysis of the ordinary notion of a cause. Counterfactual theories hold that c causes e when e counterfactually depends on c, that is, when e would not have occurred had c not occurred. Preemption occurs when a backup cause is present but does not operate because the actual cause gets there first; overdetermination occurs when two causes each independently suffice and both operate. An intervention is a change to a variable that is brought about in such a way that it is independent of the other causes of the variables it affects, which is what licenses reading a structural equation as causal. Invariance is the stability of a relationship under interventions on other variables, and it is the property that distinguishes causal from accidental generalisations.
depth.mechanism: The interventionist account turns the counterfactual into a claim about a system of equations. Variables are connected by structural equations, each equation expressing the value of one variable as a function of its causes plus an independent error term. An intervention on a variable sets its value by an operation that breaks the equation determining it, leaving every other equation intact. A causal claim then says that the relationship between two variables is invariant under interventions on the cause and on the other variables that are not on the path. Three technical consequences follow. Confounding is a common cause that makes two variables dependent without either causing the other, and it is represented by a path through a third variable; controlling for it amounts to conditioning on that variable. Conditioning on a collider, a variable caused by both members of a pair, induces dependence where there was none, which is why naive adjustment can create associations rather than remove them. And the choice of variables determines which causal questions are well formed, since a variable that is held fixed cannot be manipulated, which is why the same event can be a cause under one description and a background condition under another. These are not merely formal niceties; they are the reason lesson 98's warnings about confounders and colliders have a precise statement.
depth.secondExample: An investigator asks why a warehouse fire started. The electrical fault, the stacked cardboard, the open door, the absence of a sprinkler, and the oxygen in the air are all conditions without which the fire would not have occurred in the way it did. A regularity or INUS analysis lists them all as causes, which is correct in one sense and useless in another. Causal selection, discussed by Hart and Honoré in 'Causation in the Law' (1959), explains the difference: ordinary causal talk is contrastive, and the answer depends on the contrast class and on norms of normal functioning. If the question is why this warehouse burned rather than remaining intact, the electrical fault is the cause and the oxygen is background. If the question is why it burned rather than smouldering, the cardboard load matters. If the question is why it burned rather than being extinguished, the missing sprinkler matters. None of these answers conflicts with the others, and none is merely subjective: each is a true claim about difference-making relative to a specified contrast. The case shows that a metaphysics of causation needs an account of selection as well as an account of the relation, and it explains why legal and historical explanations can disagree about the cause of one event without either being wrong about the facts.
depth.mistake: The first error is to think preemption refutes the counterfactual theory, when it refutes only its simplest formulation; the theory has resourceful descendants and remains the dominant approach. The second is to think regularity theories are dead, when INUS analysis survives in epidemiology, engineering, and law, where the question is which conditions are components of a sufficient set. The third is to confuse causation with causal explanation or with causal attribution, so that a pragmatic fact about which cause is salient is treated as a fact about the causal relation, or the reverse, so that selection is dismissed as mere rhetoric. The fourth is to think interventionism requires a human manipulator, which would make causal claims about the early universe or about inaccessible systems impossible; Woodward's interventions can be natural processes that meet the independence condition. A diagnostic: ask what question is being answered. If it is what would happen under a change, the interventionist apparatus is appropriate; if it is which conditions were jointly sufficient, INUS analysis is appropriate; if it is what to say in an explanation, the contrastive account is appropriate, and treating one answer as the whole of causation is the error.
depth.application: Non-blocking task on paper. Draw a directed acyclic graph with five variables for a case you know, for instance study time, sleep, attendance, exam performance, and prior attainment. Then complete four steps. Step one, mark which arrows are plausible and which are reversed, and identify at least one confounder and one collider. Step two, write one causal claim in interventionist form: which variable is intervened on, which is held fixed, and what change is predicted. Step three, write the same claim as a counterfactual and state one case in which the counterfactual would hold without causation, or vice versa. Step four, write a contrastive explanation of one observed outcome and name the contrast class. Model response for the study case: prior attainment confounds study time and performance, so a raw association overstates the effect; intervening on study time while holding prior attainment fixed predicts a smaller increase; the counterfactual would fail to hold in a preemption case where a tutor's help substituted for study; the contrastive explanation of a poor result is relative to the contrast class of students with the same prior attainment. Self-review rubric: (1) the graph is acyclic and every arrow has a stated justification; (2) the intervention is described as breaking an equation, not as merely changing a value; (3) the counterfactual and the interventionist formulation are shown to agree or the disagreement is explained; (4) the contrast class is named explicitly rather than left to context.
depth.summary: Causation is not one thing but a family of related notions, and the theories on offer are answers to different questions about it. Regularity tells you which conditions were jointly sufficient, counterfactual dependence tells you what made a difference, and intervention tells you what would change under a manipulation, while selection tells you which difference is worth reporting. The discipline this lesson teaches is to ask which of these a causal claim is making before asking whether it is true, because a claim that is false under one reading can be true under another. Lesson 108 turns to a relation that is even more pervasive and even harder to state, the relation of one time to another.

lessons.title: Time: McTaggart's argument, the A and B series, and the reality of passage
lessons.explanation: Lessons 106 and 107 treated necessity and causation as relations that hold between things, and both presupposed an order of times over which worlds and causal chains are spread. This lesson asks what that order is. McTaggart's 'The Unreality of Time' (Mind, 1908) is the most discussed argument in the philosophy of time, and it is usually misreported as a proof that time does not exist. Its structure is more interesting. McTaggart distinguishes three orderings. The A series orders events as past, present, and future, and it is dynamic, since events move through these positions. The B series orders events as earlier than, simultaneous with, and later than, and it is static, since those relations never change. The C series is the bare B series stripped of direction. His argument has two stages. First, the A series is essential to time, because change requires something to become past or future, and a world with only B relations would be a frozen block without change, so no time. Second, the A series is contradictory: every event is past, present, and future, and these properties are incompatible, so the A series cannot be real. The standard reply, that an event is present now, was future, and will be past, is said to fail because it re-introduces A-series terms ('now', 'will be') at the level of the explanation, so the contradiction is not resolved but postponed, generating a regress. McTaggart concludes that time is unreal. The contemporary debate takes the two stages separately. B-theorists accept the first stage's conclusion about the A series and deny that time needs it, analysing tense as a relation between an utterance and an event. A-theorists defend the A series, either by holding that temporal properties are had relative to times, or by treating the tensed copula as primitive.
lessons.example: Take a single event, the first performance of a particular symphony in 1900. According to the A series, it was future in 1899, is past now, and was present in 1900. McTaggart's charge is that the event is thus characterised by three incompatible properties, pastness, presentness, and futurity, which cannot be true of one thing at once. The natural reply is that the properties are had at different times: the event is present in 1900 and past in 2026, and there is no contradiction because the predicates are time-indexed. McTaggart's counter-reply is that the indexing itself uses A-series vocabulary. To say the event is present at 1900 is to say that 1900 is now, or that the event is present when 1900 is present, and that 'when' is either an A-series notion, in which case the contradiction recurs, or a B-series notion, in which case the A series has been abandoned. The regress is generated because each attempt to resolve the contradiction by placing the incompatible properties at different times must specify those times in tensed terms. Whether the regress is vicious is the crux. Dummett, in 'Bringing About the Past' (1964), took the argument seriously enough to reconstruct it as a proof that the A series cannot be a feature of reality, and later defences of tense, such as Lowe's, reply that tensed facts are irreducible and that the demand for a further time at which they hold is a category mistake. The disagreement is genuine: the argument is valid on some readings and question-begging on others, and the reader should be able to say which premise is being denied rather than merely that the conclusion is unwelcome.
lessons.question: A reader concludes from McTaggart's argument that time is an illusion and that nothing is really earlier than anything else. On the argument's own structure, what does it actually establish, and what does the reader's conclusion add?
lessons.answer: If sound, it establishes that the A series cannot be fundamental; the further claim that B relations are unreal is McTaggart's own additional premise, and a B-theorist accepts the first result while rejecting the second
lessons.distractor: If sound, it establishes that both series are unreal, since time requires the A series and McTaggart has shown the A series to be contradictory
lessons.correction: That inference needs the premise that the B series cannot constitute time on its own, which is precisely what B-theorists deny and what McTaggart argues for separately, and weakly. The reader has taken the author's conclusion for the argument's only upshot, the recurring error of reading a regress argument as though a local impossibility were a global one.

depth.definitions: The A series is the ordering of events as past, present, and future, together with the property of being present at a particular time. The B series is the ordering of events by the relations earlier than, simultaneous with, and later than. Presentism is the thesis that only present things exist; eternalism is the thesis that past, present, and future things all exist equally; the growing block theory holds that the past and present exist and the future does not, so reality grows. The moving spotlight theory combines eternalism with a single privileged present that shifts along the block. Tense is the linguistic expression of A-series position, as in 'was', 'is', and 'will be'. A token-reflexive expression is one whose reference depends on the token utterance, such as 'now', analysed as 'simultaneous with this utterance'. Temporal passage is the supposed movement of events from future to present to past, or equivalently the movement of the present along the series of events.
depth.mechanism: The B-theoretic response works by reduction. Tense is analysed in terms of B relations and the position of the utterance: 'the symphony is past' means that the performance is earlier than this utterance, and 'it will rain' means that rain is later than this utterance. On that analysis no event has the property of presentness simpliciter, so the contradiction McTaggart identifies never arises, and change is analysed as a difference in properties across B-related times: the iron is hot at t1 and cold at t2, which is change enough. The cost is that passage becomes a feature of experience rather than of the world; nothing literally moves from future to past, and the sense that time flows is explained by the fact that our experiences are themselves distributed in the block. The A-theoretic response accepts that tense is irreducible and denies that temporal properties are had simpliciter, holding instead that they are had relative to a time, with the relativisation not itself requiring a further time. The cost there is that the present acquires a privileged status that physics does not obviously support, and presentism in particular has to explain how claims about the past and future can be true when the entities they concern do not exist. Both responses are coherent; the dispute turns on which cost is acceptable, and on whether the special theory of relativity permits a privileged present at all.
depth.secondExample: Aristotle's discussion in 'De Interpretatione' chapter 9 poses a different problem about time and truth. He considers the statement 'there will be a sea battle tomorrow'. If every statement is either true or false, then either the statement or its negation is true now, and if one is true now, the battle is already settled, so nothing depends on anyone's deliberation. The argument threatens not the reality of tense but the openness of the future. Aristotle's own solution restricts the principle of bivalence for statements about contingent future events, so that neither the affirmation nor the denial is yet true or false. Later solutions divide into two families. One rejects future excluded middle, using three-valued or branching-time semantics, as in Lukasiewicz's system and in Prior's work on tense logic. The other keeps bivalence and rejects the necessity of the past, holding that what is true at a moment may depend on how the future unfolds, which is the Ockhamist and 'thin red line' approach. The case is worth separating from McTaggart's because it shows that the reality of tense and the openness of the future are independent questions: one can hold a B-theoretic block and still ask whether the block contains one future or many, and one can be a presentist and still be a fatalist.
depth.mistake: The first error is to think McTaggart's conclusion simply follows, when the argument's second stage is contested and the B-theoretic reply denies a premise rather than the conclusion. The second is to think B-theory denies change. It denies passage, that is, the movement of a privileged present, but it analyses change as variation across B-related times, which is why a B-theorist can say without irony that the milk has turned. The third is to equate the A theory with presentism. Growing block and moving spotlight are A-theories that take the past or the whole block to exist, and conflating them with presentism makes the debate look like a choice between common sense and physics. The fourth is to confuse the experience of passage with passage itself: the fact that time seems to flow is a datum for psychology and for the philosophy of perception, and it is compatible with a block universe in which nothing flows, provided the experiences are themselves located at different times. Diagnostics: when a verdict about time is offered, ask whether it concerns existence, tense, or experience, because the three come apart and arguments for one do not settle the others.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose three statements: one about the past, one about the future, and one expressing change, for instance 'the bridge was built in 1890', 'the river will flood again', and 'the metal cooled'. For each, write three lines. Line one, the A-series rendering, with tense made explicit. Line two, the B-series rendering, using only earlier, later, and simultaneous, plus the position of the utterance. Line three, a verdict on whether anything is lost in the translation, and if something is, whether it is a fact about the world or a fact about our perspective. Then add a fourth line identifying which premise of McTaggart's argument you would deny, and why. Model response for the future statement: in A terms, the flood is future; in B terms, the flood is later than this utterance; what is lost is the sense that the future is unsettled, which may be a fact about our epistemic position rather than about the world, and the denial is of the premise that the A series is essential to time. Self-review rubric: (1) the B-series rendering contains no tensed verbs except those describing the utterance; (2) the verdict distinguishes what is lost in translation from what is merely expressed differently; (3) the denied premise is named rather than gestured at; (4) at least one case is considered where the A and B renderings differ in truth value, since those are the cases that decide between the theories.
depth.summary: The philosophy of time is organised by one distinction and one argument. The distinction between the A series and the B series separates the dynamic and static aspects of temporal order; the argument is McTaggart's, and its lasting value is that it forces a choice between treating tense as fundamental and treating it as a feature of how things are described. Neither choice is free. The A-theorist pays in privileged presents and in trouble with relativity; the B-theorist pays in passage and in the awkwardness of saying that nothing really happens. The discipline is to state which cost one is accepting, rather than to announce that time is or is not real. Lesson 109 moves from time to matter and asks a question of the same shape about objects: when do parts compose a whole?

lessons.title: Composition and the Problem of the Many: when do parts make a whole?
lessons.explanation: Lesson 97 established that vague predicates generate sorites pressure, and that the pressure can be handled by supervaluationism, by many-valued logic, or by denying that vagueness is a feature of the world. This lesson applies the same pressure to a different subject: not to whether a predicate applies, but to whether an object exists. Van Inwagen's 'Material Beings' (1990) names the question the special composition question: under what conditions do some things compose a further thing? Three families of answer compete. Nihilism holds that composition never occurs, so there are simples and nothing composed of them. Universalism holds that composition always occurs, so any plurality whatsoever has a sum. Restricted views hold that composition occurs under some condition, for instance when the parts are in contact, or when they constitute a life. Van Inwagen himself defends a restricted view on which a plurality composes something exactly when its activity constitutes a life. The Problem of the Many, developed by Unger in 'The Problem of the Many' (1980) and anticipated by Geach's Tibbles puzzle (1966), sharpens the issue. Any ordinary object has a boundary that is not sharply determined, since a single hair or molecule more or less makes no difference to whether something is a cat. If composition is unrestricted, every candidate aggregate of molecules that differs by one hair is a composed object, and each seems equally entitled to be called the cat. Either there is no unique cat, or the boundaries are determined after all, or composition is restricted in a way that rules most candidates out.
lessons.example: Consider a cat asleep on a mat. Take the set of molecules that make up the cat, and consider a second set that differs by one molecule at the tip of a hair, and a third that differs by two, and so on. Every one of these sets is a candidate to be the cat, because the difference between them is far below the threshold at which anything about cat behaviour or cat biology changes. If composition is unrestricted, every candidate set composes an object, so there are billions of cat-shaped objects on the mat, all occupying almost exactly the same region. Now ask which of them is the cat. There is no principled answer: any criterion that selects one will be arbitrary with respect to the differences among them, and any criterion that selects none leaves us without a cat. The argument is a reductio with several escape routes. One may deny unrestricted composition and hold that only some pluralities compose, which requires saying which and defending the line. One may accept that there are many overlapping objects and hold that counting is relative to a concept, so that 'how many cats' has an answer only relative to a sortal. One may hold that the vagueness is epistemic, a matter of our ignorance of a sharp boundary, though this sits awkwardly with the thought that a single molecule cannot make the difference between being a cat and not. Or one may accept nihilism and treat cats as useful fictions about simples arranged cat-wise.
lessons.question: An argument concludes that because there is no principled boundary between the candidate aggregates that might be the cat, there are no cats, only cat-shaped swarms. What does the argument actually establish, and which further premise does the conclusion need?
lessons.answer: It establishes that unrestricted composition plus a demand for a unique boundary is unstable; the nihilist conclusion needs the further premise that no restriction of composition or relativisation of counting is defensible
lessons.distractor: It establishes nihilism directly, since once the boundaries are shown to be vague the only consistent position is that composed objects do not exist
lessons.correction: Vagueness at the boundary is compatible with several responses, including restricted composition and concept-relative counting, and the argument does not choose among them. The learner's error is to treat a reductio of a package of views as a proof of one particular member, which is the same mistake as reading McTaggart's argument as a proof of the unreality of the B series.

depth.definitions: Composition is the relation that holds between some things and a whole they make up. The special composition question asks for the conditions under which composition occurs; the general composition question asks what composition is. Nihilism denies that composition ever occurs; universalism affirms that it always does; restricted views affirm that it occurs under some specified condition. A simple is an object with no proper parts. A sortal is a concept that supplies a criterion of identity and counting, such as 'cat' or 'statue'. Coincidence is the relation between two objects that occupy the same region at the same time without being identical, as a statue and the lump of bronze that constitutes it. Constitution is the relation that is supposed to hold in such cases, as when a lump constitutes a statue. Four-dimensionalism holds that persisting objects have temporal parts, so that a cat is a sum of cat-stages; three-dimensionalism holds that objects are wholly present at each time at which they exist.
depth.mechanism: Sider's argument from vagueness (in 'Four-Dimensionalism', 2001) runs as follows. Suppose composition sometimes occurs. Then there is a series of cases, from a clear case of composition to a clear case of non-composition, differing by imperceptible increments, for instance by the addition of one molecule at a time to a scattered plurality. If composition sometimes occurs and sometimes does not, there must be a cutoff somewhere in that series. But existence is not a vague matter: either a thing exists or it does not, and there is no such thing as a thing's existence being indeterminate. Since no cutoff can be non-arbitrary, there is no such cutoff, so composition either always occurs or never does. The argument is valid, and its conclusion is a dilemma: universalism or nihilism. Everything then turns on the premise that existence cannot be vague. If one accepts ontic vagueness, the argument fails and restricted views become available again. If one denies ontic vagueness, one must choose between the two extremes and explain away the appearance of middle cases, which is what van Inwagen does by treating talk of chairs as talk about simples arranged chair-wise. The Problem of the Many is the mirror image: it starts from the vagueness of boundaries and derives a proliferation of objects rather than a dilemma about composition, and the two arguments together constrain the space of acceptable views more tightly than either does alone.
depth.secondExample: A bronze statue stands in a courtyard. The lump of bronze was cast in 1900 and the statue was created at the same moment; if the statue is later melted down, the bronze survives as a lump while the statue ceases to exist. The statue and the lump occupy exactly the same region, are made of exactly the same molecules, and yet appear to differ in their modal properties: the statue could not survive being flattened, while the lump could. This is the coincidence problem, discussed by Gibbard in 'Contingent Identity' (1975) and by Baker in 'Persons and Bodies' (2000). Three responses are available. One denies that there are two things, holding that 'statue' and 'lump' are different ways of describing one object, which requires explaining away the modal difference. One accepts two coincident objects and analyses the difference in terms of different persistence conditions, which requires a principled account of when constitution occurs. One adopts four-dimensionalism, so that the statue and the lump are different sums of temporal parts, overlapping for the period of their coexistence, which makes coincidence a matter of shared parts rather than of shared regions. The case is a useful test of any theory of composition, because it isolates the question of identity from the question of material constitution, and because each response has a cost that the others avoid.
depth.mistake: The first error is to move from vagueness in our concepts to vagueness in the world without argument, which is the move lesson 97 warned against and which the Problem of the Many exploits. The second is to think nihilism is refuted by the obvious existence of cats. Nihilism is a thesis about composition, not about appearance, and van Inwagen's paraphrase strategy, according to which there are simples arranged cat-wise, is designed to preserve everything we want to say at the level of ordinary discourse. The third is to think the Problem of the Many shows that nothing exists, when its conclusion is that a combination of unrestricted composition and sharp counting is untenable, and that one of the conjuncts must give. The fourth is to treat the special composition question as verbal, on the grounds that different answers use 'object' differently. That may be true, but it is a substantive claim that needs argument, since if the question is verbal then the disputes about statues and persons that depend on it are verbal too, which is a large consequence to accept on the strength of a linguistic observation.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose a scene with several contested objects, for instance a kitchen with a table, a cup, a crack in the cup, and a pile of crumbs. Complete four steps. Step one, list the candidate objects and, for each, the plurality of simples that would compose it. Step two, apply each of the three answers to the special composition question and record which candidates exist under each. Step three, run the Problem of the Many on one candidate, specifying the series of aggregates that differ by one molecule and asking where the cutoff falls. Step four, state which answer you find most defensible and what you have to give up to hold it. Model response for the cup: under nihilism there are simples arranged cup-wise and no cup; under universalism there are indefinitely many cup-like sums, including sums that include the crack and sums that do not; under a restricted view there is one cup if the restriction is satisfied, and the restriction must be stated; the Problem of the Many shows that the universalist cannot say which sum is the cup without a sortal-relative counting rule. Self-review rubric: (1) each candidate is described by its parts, not just named; (2) the three answers are applied consistently rather than mixed; (3) the series in step three is genuinely gradual, with no smuggled sharp boundary; (4) the cost accepted in step four is stated as a cost, not as a virtue.
depth.summary: Two arguments constrain the metaphysics of objects. The argument from vagueness says that composition cannot be vague, so it either always or never occurs, and since we exist it always does. The Problem of the Many says that boundaries are vague, so either there are many objects where we thought there was one or counting is relative to a concept. Together they force a choice between universalism with relative counting, nihilism with paraphrase, and a restricted view that must specify its restriction without arbitrariness. The lesson's transferable skill is the ability to hold both arguments in view at once, since each is easy to answer in isolation and hard to answer together. Lesson 110 asks what to do when a dispute of this kind cannot be settled by argument about the world, and whether the right response is to revise the concepts instead.

lessons.title: Capstone: conceptual engineering, or revising the question instead of answering it
lessons.explanation: This level has produced three results that now need to be combined. Lesson 101 showed that meaning has layers, so a term can be replaced by a co-referential one without preserving what was said. Lesson 105 showed that meaning is partly external, fixed by environments, experts, and institutions rather than by the speaker's concepts. Lessons 106 to 109 showed that several central metaphysical disputes, about worlds, essences, objects, and composition, may turn on which framework or which counting convention is adopted rather than on which side has discovered a fact. Carnap drew the consequence in 'Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology' (1950). He distinguished internal questions, which are asked and answered within a linguistic framework by its own rules, from external questions, which are practical questions about whether to adopt the framework at all. Whether there are numbers is, internally, answered by arithmetic; the external question is whether to speak the arithmetical language, and it is settled by convenience, not by truth. Carnap's method for replacing a vague term with a precise one is explication, set out in the first chapter of 'Logical Foundations of Probability' (1950). Quine's 'On What There Is' (1948) and 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951) reply that the internal/external distinction depends on a sharp analytic/synthetic boundary that cannot be drawn, so framework choice is continuous with ordinary theory choice. Haslanger's ameliorative analysis, in 'Gender and Race' (2000) and 'Resisting Reality' (2012), adds a normative dimension: the question is not only what a concept means but what it ought to mean, given the purposes it serves.
lessons.example: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union adopted a definition of 'planet' requiring that a body orbit the sun, have sufficient mass for hydrostatic equilibrium, and have cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. Pluto satisfies the first two conditions and fails the third, so it was reclassified as a dwarf planet. The episode is a worked example of explication. The prior usage was vague at the boundaries: the word applied clearly to Jupiter and Mars and less clearly to objects in the Kuiper belt, and there was no fact of the matter about Pluto that the vote revealed. Carnap's four criteria for a good explication can be applied directly. Similarity requires the new term to capture most of the old term's clear cases, and the definition does, since the eight planets remain planets. Exactness requires a precise criterion, and orbital clearance, whatever its measurement difficulties, is precise in principle. Fruitfulness requires the term to support classification and theory, and the three-class scheme, planets, dwarf planets, and small solar system bodies, does. Simplicity is the weakest link, since the clearance criterion requires an arbitrary mass threshold for the neighbourhood. The costs are equally visible. The redefinition broke topic continuity for ordinary speakers, since school textbooks and museum displays had used the word for seventy years in a way that included Pluto, and it created a category, dwarf planet, whose name contains the very word it was supposed to replace. A defender of the decision must argue that the classificatory gain outweighs the discontinuity, and that argument is normative, not empirical.
lessons.question: A committee redefines a contested term for administrative purposes. A critic objects that the old meaning was the correct one and the new definition is therefore false. A second critic objects that since the definition is a decision, any definition is as good as any other. Assess both objections.
lessons.answer: Both fail: the first treats a decision as a discovery of an essence, and the second ignores the constraints that make explication assessable, namely similarity to prior usage, exactness, fruitfulness, and continuity of topic
lessons.distractor: The first fails and the second succeeds, since once a term is acknowledged to be conventional there is no standard by which one definition can be better than another
lessons.correction: Conventionality is compatible with assessment. A specification can be judged better or worse at serving the purpose for which it was adopted, at preserving the cases that any successor concept must preserve, and at supporting the inferences the term was introduced to support. The distractor moves from 'not discovered' to 'not evaluable', which is the same slide as concluding that because a measurement is a human construction, one measurement is as good as another.

depth.definitions: Conceptual engineering is the deliberate revision of a concept or term for theoretical or practical purposes. Explication, in Carnap's sense, is the replacement of a vague or pretheoretical term by a precise one, assessed by similarity to prior usage, exactness, fruitfulness, and simplicity. An internal question is asked within an accepted framework and answered by its rules; an external question concerns whether to adopt the framework, and Carnap treats it as a practical question about convenience. Ameliorative analysis, in Haslanger's sense, asks what a concept should be given the purposes it is meant to serve, as opposed to descriptive analysis, which asks what the concept is. Topic continuity is the constraint that a revised term must still be about the same subject matter, so that the revision is a change in the concept rather than a change of topic. Semantic externalism, from lesson 105, is the thesis that meaning is partly fixed by factors outside the speaker, which constrains how far a reformer can change a term by declaration.
depth.mechanism: Carnap's picture separates two kinds of disagreement. Within a framework, claims have truth values and disagreements are settled by the framework's rules; between frameworks, there is no common standard of truth, only a comparison of the frameworks' utility for specified purposes. Quine's objection is that the separation cannot be maintained, because the boundary between analytic truths, which hold by meaning, and synthetic truths, which hold by fact, is itself a matter of degree and of holistic adjustment. If Quine is right, framework choice is continuous with empirical theory choice, and the difference between internal and external questions is one of scale rather than of kind. Haslanger's method takes a further step by building the purpose into the analysis. Descriptive analysis reports the concept's extension and inferential role; ameliorative analysis asks what the concept is for, and proposes a replacement that serves that function better. The proposal is assessed by its consequences, which makes the method normative from the start, and this is why the objection that it is political rather than philosophical misses the point: the question of what a concept ought to do is a normative question, and it needs normative argument. The externalist constraint from lesson 105 supplies the limit on the method, since a reformer cannot simply decree a new extension; she has to change usage, training, and institutions, and the term's causal history will drag some of the old reference along with it.
depth.secondExample: Consider the concept of death. The Harvard Ad Hoc Committee's 1968 report proposed irreversible coma, defined by the absence of brain function, as a criterion of death, and most jurisdictions now treat irreversible loss of all brain function as sufficient, while a few permit religious objection to that criterion. The case is instructive because the dispute is not about a natural kind awaiting discovery but about which criterion follows from the concept of death, and the candidates, circulatory, whole-brain, and brainstem, are not merely verbal variants. Each carries different implications for when ventilation may be withdrawn, when a death certificate may be issued, and when organs may be procured. An ameliorative analysis asks what the concept of death is for: if it marks the point at which a person ceases to exist, then the criterion should track the irreversible loss of the capacity for consciousness and for integrated bodily function; if it marks the point at which a body may be treated as a corpse, the criterion may be different. The case also shows why explication cannot be a matter of stipulation. A definition that counted reversible coma as death would fail similarity to prior usage so badly that it would no longer be a concept of death, and it would license inferences, such as withdrawal of treatment from a patient who will recover, that the prior concept existed to block. The practical stakes make the choice consequential, and the argument for a criterion therefore has to be given in normative and biological terms at once.
depth.mistake: The first error is Humpty Dumpty's, that a term means whatever its user chooses. Semantic externalism and the division of linguistic labour make this false for most terms, and topic continuity makes it self-defeating, since a word redefined at will no longer refers to the thing anyone was arguing about. The second error is the converse, that because meaning is social, no individual or institution can revise a concept, which overstates the constraint: revision is possible through changes in usage, training, and institutional rules, as the history of 'planet', 'marriage', and 'death' shows. The third is to conflate descriptive and ameliorative analysis, so that a proposal about what a concept ought to be is criticised for misreporting what it is, or a report is welcomed as a recommendation. The fourth is to think that a normative conclusion follows from a conceptual analysis alone. An ameliorative analysis can show that a proposed concept serves a purpose better, but it cannot show that the purpose is worth serving without a further argument, and that argument is where the real disagreement usually lies.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose one contested term in a domain you know, such as 'poverty', 'species', 'addiction', 'refugee', or 'algorithmic bias'. Write four sections. Section one, descriptive analysis: the term's clear cases, its borderline cases, and the inferential commitments speakers take on when they use it. Section two, functional analysis: what the term is used to do, naming at least two purposes that may conflict. Section three, an ameliorative proposal: a precise criterion, with a note on which clear cases it preserves and which it revises. Section four, a cost table with rows for similarity, exactness, fruitfulness, simplicity, and topic continuity, each with a sentence of verdict. Model response for 'poverty': the descriptive analysis centres on material deprivation relative to a standard; the functions include identifying need, allocating transfers, and comparing across countries; the proposal might be a relative measure indexed to median income; the cost table records high fruitfulness for policy, moderate similarity, and a controversial discontinuity for countries at different income levels. Self-review rubric: (1) the descriptive section reports usage rather than recommending; (2) the purposes are distinguished and not merged into a single slogan; (3) the proposal is precise enough that a disputed case can be decided; (4) the costs are stated as costs, and the normative argument for the purpose is identified as a separate step rather than assumed.
depth.summary: Conceptual engineering is what is left to do when a dispute turns out to be about the framework rather than about the facts within it. Its instruments are explication, which trades vagueness for precision at a measurable cost in continuity, and ameliorative analysis, which asks what a concept is for and proposes a replacement that serves the purpose better. Its constraints come from the earlier lessons in this level: meaning is layered, so a redefinition will not capture everything the old term did; meaning is external, so revision requires changing usage rather than announcing a definition; and the disputes of metaphysics are often disputes about which framework to use, which makes the choice of framework a practical question that still has better and worse answers. The level therefore ends where philosophy usually begins again, with the recognition that describing our concepts and deciding which concepts to have are different tasks, and that both are needed.

readings.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rudolf Carnap', sections 1 'General Characterization' and 7 'Quine and Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology'
readings.note: Section 1 introduces the linguistic-framework picture and the principle of tolerance, and section 7 reconstructs the exchange with Quine over internal and external questions, which is the hinge of this lesson. Read section 6 on semantics and modality if you want to see why Carnap needed the framework distinction in the first place. The entry is a survey of a large body of work; the sections named are the ones that bear on conceptual revision.

readings.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Feminist Metaphysics', section 1.1.3 'Ameliorative Inquiry' and section 2.3 'Metametaphysics'
readings.note: Section 1.1.3 sets out Haslanger's ameliorative method as a response to the debunking project, which is the clearest short statement of the distinction between descriptive and ameliorative analysis. Section 2.3 connects the method to metametaphysics, which is where the question of what metaphysical inquiry is for gets asked. Read section 1.1.1 on idea and object construction first, since the vocabulary of social construction is used throughout. The entry is a survey of a contested field and reports positions it does not endorse.

readings.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction', sections 3.4 'Verificationism and Confirmation Holism' and 3.6 'Explaining Away the Appearance of the Analytic'
readings.note: Section 3.4 states Quine's holism and its consequences for the analytic/synthetic boundary, which is the objection that any sharp internal/external distinction must answer. Section 3.6 surveys the attempts to explain the appearance of analyticity without the distinction. Read section 4 for the post-Quinean strategies, especially 4.2 on externalist theories of meaning, which is where lesson 105's material enters.

visual.title: Internal question, external question, and the explication loop
visual.description: A diagram separating questions asked inside a framework from the choice of framework, with the four explication criteria as an evaluation loop.
steps: Framework box: a language with rules, including a term such as 'planet' or 'death', and internal questions answerable by those rules
Internal question: does this body satisfy the criterion? Answered by observation and by the framework's definitions, with a truth value
External question: should we use this framework at all? Answered by comparison of purposes, not by truth, on Carnap's account
Quinean objection node: the boundary between the two is not sharp, because analyticity is not a determinate category, so the external question shades into theory choice
Explication loop: propose a precise criterion, then evaluate it on similarity to prior usage, exactness, fruitfulness, and simplicity
Topic continuity gate: if the revised term no longer tracks the prior subject matter, the proposal is a change of topic rather than an explication, and the gate sends it back
Normative exit: the choice of purpose is defended by argument, since an ameliorative analysis can show that a concept serves a purpose better but cannot show that the purpose is worth serving

questions.prompt: An essay argues: 'There is a possible world in which you have a sister, so you have a sister in that world, and therefore a sister exists.' A critic says the conclusion does not follow, but a modal realist insists that all possible worlds are as concrete as the actual one. Who is right, and why?
questions.answer: The critic is right: 'there is a world where P' quantifies over worlds, and existence at a world is not existence in the actual world; even on concretism, actuality is indexical and the sister is not among the things here
questions.distractor: The modal realist is right, because if all worlds are equally concrete then whatever exists at any world exists without qualification, and actuality is a mere honorific
questions.correction: Concretism is a thesis about what worlds are, not about what exists here; Lewis pairs it with counterpart theory and an indexical analysis of actuality precisely so that 'possibly a sister exists' does not entail that a sister exists. The distractor conflates existence at a world with existence simpliciter, which is the restriction the quantifier is there to enforce.

questions.prompt: Suzy throws a rock that shatters a bottle; Billy throws too, but his rock arrives a fraction later and would have shattered the bottle had Suzy missed. A lawyer argues that Suzy did not cause the shattering, because had she not thrown the bottle would still have shattered. Assess the argument.
questions.answer: Its second premise is true but its conclusion does not follow as a claim about causation: Suzy's throw is a cause, so counterfactual dependence is not necessary for causation and the theory needs supplementing, for instance by influence or a contrastive formulation
questions.distractor: It is sound: causation just is counterfactual dependence, so where the effect would have occurred anyway there is no causation, and the later throw is the cause
questions.correction: This is the standard preemption counterexample to the simple counterfactual theory, and the distractor accepts the theory's verdict instead of testing it against the case. The practical cost is visible: the reasoning would exonerate the actual producer whenever a redundant backup exists, which inverts the purpose of a causal inquiry.

questions.prompt: McTaggart argues that every event is past, present, and future, that these properties are incompatible, and that the reply that an event is present only now and future later generates a regress. A reader concludes that time is an illusion and that nothing is really earlier than anything else. Where does the argument actually leave the dispute?
questions.answer: If sound it shows the A series cannot be fundamental; a B-theorist accepts that verdict and keeps the B series as real, so the conclusion that nothing is earlier than anything else does not follow
questions.distractor: If sound it shows temporal relations are unreal, since time needs both series and McTaggart has undermined the A series
questions.correction: McTaggart drew the stronger conclusion himself, but his argument against the A series is compatible with realism about the B series, which is the standard reply. The reader has taken the author's conclusion for the argument's only upshot, a recurring error in reading regress arguments, where a local impossibility is inflated into a global one.

questions.prompt: Take a cat. Each of the billions of candidate aggregates of molecules differing from the cat's molecules by a single hair at the boundary seems equally qualified to be the cat, and there is no principled line at which a candidate stops being the cat. A philosopher concludes that there are no cats, only cat-shaped swarms. Assess the conclusion.
questions.answer: It does not follow: the argument shows that unrestricted composition plus a demand for a unique boundary is unstable, and the alternatives include restricting composition, accepting ontic vagueness, or treating counting as concept-relative
questions.distractor: It follows, because vagueness is always a defect of language, and once language is corrected the swarm is all that remains
questions.correction: That move assumes the epistemic view of vagueness and then helps itself to an ontological conclusion, which the view forbids. Even granting many candidates, nihilism is one response among several; the learner's error is to treat a reductio of a package of views as a proof of one particular member.

questions.prompt: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined 'planet' so as to exclude Pluto. A textbook author objects that Pluto was a planet before 2006 and that the new definition is therefore false to the facts, while a committee member replies that the definition was adopted because a three-class scheme serves classification better. What is the dispute about?
questions.answer: About which concept to use for a purpose, not about a hidden essence; the redefinition is an explication assessed by similarity to prior usage, exactness, and fruitfulness, and its cost is a break in topic continuity
questions.distractor: About an essence that astronomers discovered in 2006, so the textbook author is simply wrong about what 'planet' always meant
questions.correction: The distractor treats a decision as a discovery; the earlier extension was fixed by loose usage, not by an essence awaiting detection. The opposite error is equally common: concluding that because the choice is purposive, any stipulation is as good as another, which ignores what is lost when a term no longer tracks its former topic.

questions.prompt: Two students dispute whether 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' is trivial. One says it must be, since it says of one object that it is itself; the other says it was a real astronomical discovery. Assess both claims.
questions.answer: Both are right about different things: the statement is necessary because it identifies an object with itself, yet it was discovered empirically and expresses a different thought from 'Hesperus is Hesperus', since the two names present the object differently
questions.distractor: The first student is right, because a necessary identity is knowable a priori by anyone who understands the names, so the astronomers discovered nothing
questions.correction: Necessity is a property of the proposition, not of our route to knowing it; Kripke's necessary a posteriori is exactly the case where the identity could not have failed yet could only be established by investigation. The distractor infers epistemology from metaphysics, which the whole distinction is designed to block.

questions.prompt: At a party a speaker says 'the man in the corner drinking a martini is a famous logician', indicating a man who is in fact drinking water. The man is a famous logician. A listener objects that the sentence is false because the description misdescribes him. Assess the objection.
questions.answer: On Donnellan's referential use the speaker referred to that man, and the predication is true of him, so the assertion can be true even though the description is false of the referent; the attributive reading gives a different verdict
questions.distractor: The objection is right: because the description is false of the man, no reference was achieved and the sentence is false under every analysis
questions.correction: The distractor assumes Russell's attributive analysis is the only analysis, which is precisely what Donnellan's distinction denies, and it treats a false description as a failure to refer when the referential use is designed to show the two can come apart. Note the honest limit: Donnellan's distinction is contested, and semantic accounts that treat 'the' as a presupposition trigger explain the data differently.

questions.prompt: A couple exchange vows before a friend who has no licence to solemnise marriages, believing him to be authorised. The friend declares them married. A later dispute turns on whether a marriage occurred. Using the vocabulary of speech acts, assess.
questions.answer: The illocutionary act misfires: the words had locutionary meaning and may have had perlocutionary effects, but a declarative of this kind requires authority among its felicity conditions, so no marriage was effected
questions.distractor: A marriage occurred, because the couple sincerely intended to marry and sincerity is the condition that matters for a performative
questions.correction: Sincerity is one felicity condition among several, and Austin separates it from the preparatory conditions that include the speaker's standing to perform the act. The distractor collapses all conditions into intention, which would make any sufficiently sincere utterance efficacious and would empty the notion of an institutional fact.

questions.prompt: A carpenter makes a table from a particular block of oak. A philosopher says the table could have been made from a different block, since we can imagine a workshop in which a different block is used. Assess the inference.
questions.answer: Conceivability is a fallible guide: on origin essentialism the table could not have come from a different block, though it could have been stained differently, and the intuition that it could is disputed rather than decisive
questions.distractor: The inference is sound, because whatever can be imagined without contradiction is possible, so conceivability entails possibility
questions.correction: The entailment from conceivability to possibility is exactly what Kripke's cases of the necessary a posteriori bring into question, since water could be imagined as a substance other than H2O only by imagining a different substance. Note also the honest state of the dispute: origin essentialism is widely but not universally accepted, and its critics offer counterpart-theoretic and conventionalist alternatives.

questions.prompt: A city dweller cannot tell an elm from a beech and has never seen either closely, yet uses both words correctly and asks a botanist when precision matters. A theorist concludes that she does not really mean anything by 'elm'. Assess.
questions.answer: She does mean something: her use is deferential, with the extension fixed by experts under a division of linguistic labour, so her competence does not require the ability to identify the trees
questions.distractor: The theorist is right, because meaning requires the speaker to be able to recognise the kind, and without that ability the word is empty in her idiolect
questions.correction: The distractor imposes a recognitional condition that Putnam's account explicitly rejects; the stereotype associated with a kind term is not its meaning, and reference can be borrowed. The error is to model all meaning on the first-person case, which is the assumption externalism about natural kind terms was introduced to challenge.

questions.prompt: 'Eight is necessarily greater than seven. The number of planets is eight. Therefore the number of planets is necessarily greater than seven.' A student says the conclusion is false, since there might have been five planets, and concludes the argument is invalid. Assess.
questions.answer: The conclusion is false on the de dicto reading and true on the de re reading; the argument is valid when the description takes wide scope, so the student has detected an ambiguity rather than an invalidity
questions.distractor: The argument is invalid because identity fails in modal contexts, so no term may be substituted into a modal sentence
questions.correction: Substitution is legitimate when the term refers to the object, which is what wide scope secures; the failure is a scope ambiguity, not a blanket prohibition. The distractor repeats the over-generalisation from the belief case in lesson 101, where the same local phenomenon was mistaken for a collapse of substitutivity.

questions.prompt: A barometer reading falls before every storm. A forecaster says the falling reading causes storms, and defends the claim by noting a perfect correlation, temporal priority, and spatial contiguity. Assess the claim.
questions.answer: The correlation is not causal: intervening to change the reading would not change the weather, so the relation fails an invariance test, and both are effects of a common cause in the atmosphere
questions.distractor: The claim is well supported, since constant conjunction with priority and contiguity is what a causal relation consists in
questions.correction: The distractor applies a regularity theory without the check that distinguishes causation from common-cause correlation, which is the intervention test. Lesson 98 established that association alone licenses no causal inference; this item asks what the causal relation itself requires, and the answer is that the association must be invariant under interventions on the putative cause.

questions.prompt: Two observers moving relative to one another disagree about whether two distant flashes are simultaneous. A presentist concludes that his view is untouched, since simultaneity is only a matter of description. Assess that reply.
questions.answer: It is too quick: if simultaneity is frame-relative, there is no single privileged set of simultaneous facts for presentness to select, so the presentist must either restrict the view to a frame or deny that frame-relative simultaneity is fundamental, and both moves are contested
questions.distractor: The reply is adequate, because presentism concerns what exists and relativity concerns measurement, so no physical result can bear on it
questions.correction: Presentism is a thesis about which things exist now, and 'now' is exactly what the relativity of simultaneity problematises, so the two cannot be sealed off so easily. The distractor defends a position by insulating it from evidence, which is a failure of the strongest-form principle rather than a defence of the view.

questions.prompt: An argument runs: composition cannot be vague, so for any objects either they always compose something or they never do; we exist and are composed of particles; therefore any particles whatsoever compose something. A critic replies that noses and door-knobs are absurd consequences. Assess the exchange.
questions.answer: The argument is valid and its conclusion follows from its premises; the absurdity objection targets universalism's cost rather than the inference, and the weakest premise is that composition cannot be vague, which restricted views deny
questions.distractor: The argument is invalid, because it moves from a claim about vagueness to a claim about existence without any intermediate premise
questions.correction: The intermediate premise is supplied: excluded middle over composition, then disjunctive syllogism against nihilism. The distractor mislocates the problem in the logic, when the real dispute concerns the vagueness premise and the plausibility of the counterintuitive consequences.

questions.prompt: A commission is asked whether patients with irreversible loss of all brain function are dead. One member says the question is empirical and neurology will answer it; another says it is purely a matter of word use and any answer will do. Assess both.
questions.answer: Neither is adequate: the question requires an explication of the concept of death that is answerable to prior usage and to coherent biological criteria, and the choice carries normative consequences that must be argued for rather than assumed
questions.distractor: The first member is right, since death is a biological fact and the criteria for it are discovered by physiology alone
questions.correction: Physiology supplies the criteria but not the concept that tells us which criteria are decisive, which is why the debate turns on what death is for and on the costs of revision. The second member's error is the mirror image: because the term is our concept, he concludes that any stipulation will do, ignoring the constraints of topic continuity and practical consequence.

questions.prompt: 'If you publish that story, your funding will be reviewed.' The editor calls it a prediction; the journalist calls it a threat. What does the dispute turn on, and how should it be resolved?
questions.answer: It turns on illocutionary force rather than content: the same proposition can be asserted as a prediction or issued as a conditional threat, and the resolution looks to the speaker's standing, intention, and the direction of fit, not to the words alone
questions.distractor: It turns on truth: since the conditional may well be true, the utterance is a prediction, and the journalist's reaction is a misinterpretation of its content
questions.correction: The distractor identifies force with content, which is the conflation Austin's distinction between locutionary and illocutionary acts was introduced to break. A true conditional can still be a threat, and the same sentence can be a warning, a promise, or a prediction depending on the speaker's position and design.

questions.prompt: A philosopher argues that because 'woman' is a social kind whose boundaries were fixed by contingent history, the term should be redefined to track a structural position, and that this redefinition is correct. Assess the step from the historical premise to the normative conclusion.
questions.answer: The premise supports the possibility of revision but not the particular revision: an ameliorative analysis must state the purpose the concept is to serve and defend that purpose, and its adequacy is judged by the function it performs rather than by the history alone
questions.distractor: The conclusion follows, because if a kind is socially constructed then any definition of it is equally legitimate, and the structural one is at least politically useful
questions.correction: Contingency of origin shows that a boundary is revisable, not that every revision is equally good; the distractor substitutes usefulness for argument and so cannot distinguish a defensible amelioration from a stipulation that serves whoever proposes it. Haslanger's own formulation is explicit that the analysis is offered for a purpose and must be assessed against it.
